title: Assessment of Countermovement Jump Performance in Collegiate Baseball Athletes: A Longitudinal Multilevel Modeling Approach.
abstract: Burke, AA, Saine, ND, King, EL, Fields, JB, Jagim, AR, Miller, AD, Green, BC, and Jones, MT. Assessment of countermovement jump performance in collegiate baseball athletes: A longitudinal multilevel modeling approach. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Given the length and demands of the collegiate baseball season, monitoring body composition and neuromuscular performance can help optimize load management and athlete readiness. Relationships between body composition and countermovement jump (CMJ) performance were examined during a competitive baseball season. Pitchers and position athletes (n = 32) completed pre- and post-season dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry scans and weekly CMJ testing. Countermovement jump variables included jump height (JH), reactive strength index modified, peak braking force (PBF), and peak propulsive force (PPF), all normalized to body mass (BM). Repeated-measures multivariate analyses of variance assessed time and group (pitcher vs. position player) effects. Pearson correlations evaluated associations between CMJ and body composition metrics, and hierarchical linear models (HLMs) quantified individual performance trajectories. Preseason-to-postseason reductions were observed in BM, fat free mass (FFM), JH, and PPF (p < 0.05). Peak braking force declined in pitchers, while PPF declined across both groups. Body composition showed negligible correlations with CMJ metrics, except for a moderately negative correlation between JH and body fat percentage (r = -0.52, p < 0.001). Hierarchical linear models revealed curvilinear CMJ performance trajectories (p < 0.001), with position players exhibiting lower PBF throughout the season (β = -1.47, p = 0.03) and preseason FFM positively predicting PBF (β = 0.118, p = 0.010). Findings suggest that reductions in lean mass and force output occur across the competitive season and vary by position. It is recommended that practitioners implement routine longitudinal monitoring when using CMJ and body composition assessments, as they may assist in detecting neuromuscular fatigue and guide individualized training interventions.

title: Trajectories of physical activity following digital education and exercise therapy-a longitudinal registry study among 15,197 persons with knee or hip osteoarthritis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study examined trajectories of physical activity (PA) and associated factors among individuals with knee or hip osteoarthritis (OA) participating in a digital education and exercise therapy program. We additionally compared patterns of patient-reported outcomes (PROs) across the identified trajectories.
METHODS: A longitudinal registry-based study. Individuals aged 40 + years with a diagnosis of knee or hip OA-confirmed through referral documentation or based on the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines and Swedish national criteria- participating in the digital program with responses to validated self-reported PA questions at enrolment and at least one follow-up (3-month intervals up to 1 year after enrolment) were included (n = 15,197). The recommended PA level was defined as ≥ 150 min/week of moderate to vigorous physical activity (yes/no). We used group-based trajectory modelling (GBTM) to identify distinct PA trajectories and multinomial logistic regression to explore associated factors. Changes in PROs from enrolment up to 1-year follow-up across PA trajectories were analysed using random intercept models.
RESULTS: The proportion of participants reaching the recommended PA levels rose from 51.4% (95% CI: 50.6, 52.2) at enrolment to 58.5% (57.1, 59.9) at one year. GBTM identified four distinct PA trajectories: persistently high (41.2%), persistently low (30.4%), increasing (16.5%), and declining (11.9%). Body mass index (BMI) followed by physical function were the most important factors associated with PA trajectory. All PA trajectories experienced clinically comparable improvements in PROs.
CONCLUSIONS: About 60% of participants reached or maintained recommended PA levels. The results suggest possible PA promotion by targeted strategies for individuals with higher BMI and poorer function. Comparable improvements in PROs across PA trajectories may support the provision of education and exercise therapy to all individuals with OA regardless of their PA level.

title: Role of the posterior tibial tendon in plantar pressure distribution across progressive stages of ligamentous insufficiency in a cadaveric flatfoot model.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Progressive collapsing foot deformity involves failure of both static and dynamic medial arch stabilizers. The relative timing and interaction between posterior tibial tendon dysfunction and ligamentous attenuation remain unclear. This study investigates whether the posterior tibial tendon can compensate for progressive ligament failure in distributing pressure under the foot in a cadaveric progressive collapsing foot deformity model at balanced stance.
METHODS: Eight cadaveric lower limbs underwent sequential ligament transections replicating progressive collapsing foot deformity. Plantar pressure was recorded during balanced stance using TekScan sensors under both loaded and unloaded posterior tibial tendon conditions. Axial and tendon loads mimicked physiologic forces. Medial-lateral and hindfoot-forefoot pressure ratios were analyzed using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.
FINDINGS: Unloading the posterior tibial tendon significantly increased hindfoot-to-forefoot loading ratios and shifted the center of pressure posteriorly across all ligamentous transection stages (P < 0.05). Medial-to-lateral loading for the entire foot shifted laterally only after the deltoid ligament transection (P = 0.016). In intact feet and short and long plantar ligament conditions, posterior tibial tendon unloading caused a medial shift in hindfoot force (P = 0.039 and P = 0.016, respectively).
INTERPRETATION: This study demonstrates the posterior tibial tendon plays a critical role in distributing plantar load and minimizing hindfoot overload through various stages of ligamentous failure. While posterior tibial tendon unloading consistently increased hindfoot loading, its influence on medial-lateral balance was variable. These findings support early interventions that preserve or augment posterior tibial tendon function to maintain biomechanical stability of the hindfoot.

title: Long-term endurance running training and testosterone daily variation in ageing men; a comparative cross-sectional study.
abstract: The aim of this study was to assess the relationship between long-term endurance running training and daily variation in testosterone, which is known to diminish during ageing, in a comparative, cross-sectional study. We recruited 45 male participants into four groups [young athletes (YA), young sedentary (YS), master athletes (MA) and elderly sedentary (ES)] and performed anthropometry, strength and ergometry tests. Morning (AM) and afternoon (PM) venous blood samples were collected to evaluate testosterone daily variation, sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG), cortisol and estradiol, and we calculated free testosterone, bioavailable testosterone and the free androgen index. Two-way and three-way ANOVAs followed by Bonferroni's multiple comparisons tests were performed. The free testosterone and free androgen index showed a significant PM decrease in the MA group (P = 0.0009 and 0.0021, respectively), comparable to YA and YS; however, in the ES group there was no difference between AM and PM values (both P > 0.9999). SHBG levels were significantly increased by both the age (P = 0.0001) and activity (P = 0.0016) factors, leading to a significant decrease in free testosterone, bioavailable testosterone and free androgen index. In the peak power output parameters of ergometry, expressed in both absolute and relative values, MA achieved values comparable to YS, significantly higher than ES (P = 0.0020 and P < 0.0001, respectively) and lower than YA (P < 0.0001). In conclusion, long-term endurance running training in elderly men might be associated with the presence of daily variation in free testosterone and higher performance levels in comparison to sedentary counterparts, but it might contribute to age-related changes in SHBG and related testosterone fraction levels.

title: The relationship of grip and three-point pinch strength to ball velocity and elbow varus torque in high school pitchers.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hand and forearm strength play an essential role in modulating and controlling forces across the elbow during pitching. In particular, grip and pinch strength reflect functional capacity of the flexor-pronator mass, which contributes to both performance and dynamic stability of the elbow. While diminished grip strength is often used clinically to monitor recovery following shoulder and elbow injury, values in adolescent pitchers are lacking. Furthermore, the relationship between grip and pinch strength with ball velocity and elbow varus torque remains poorly defined.
METHODS: Thirty-eight healthy high school pitchers (16.0 ± 0.9 years, 183.3 ± 6.0 cm, 78.1 ± 9.2 kg) were included in this study. Bilateral grip and three-point pinch strength were assessed prior to pitching. Pitchers were then analyzed using 3D motion capture (480 Hz) and ball velocity was recorded with Trackman throwing fastballs. The pitch with the greatest ball velocity was used in the analysis. Paired t-tests compared dominant and non-dominant grip and pinch strength, and linear regression examined relationships between strength, ball velocity, and elbow torque (α = 0.05).
RESULTS: Dominant arm grip strength was greater than the non-dominant throwing arm (P = .001), while pinch strength showed no side to side differences (P = .696). Dominant grip strength demonstrated weak associations with height (r2 = 0.221, P = .002), weight (r2 = 0.217, P = .002), and ball velocity (r2 = 0.116, P = .021). No significant relationships were found between grip strength and elbow varus torque. Pinch strength was not associated with height, weight, age, elbow varus torque, or ball velocity.
DISCUSSION: While forearm musculature is thought to enhance medial elbow stability, grip and pinch strength were not associated with elbow varus torque in high school pitchers. These results suggest that static hand strength measures may not reflect the complex, dynamic demands placed on the elbow during pitching. Further evaluation may be necessary to determine secondary impact such as load and subsequent fatigue on the flexor pronator complex.
CONCLUSION: Grip and pinch strength values in high school pitchers may serve as reference data for clinicians assessing adolescent pitchers. Grip strength demonstrated a weak association with ball velocity; however, neither grip nor pinch strength was significantly related to elbow loading. This highlights the need for future work examining dynamic forearm muscle function in injury risk, recovery, and performance.

title: Technical evaluation of transport-derived movement trajectories during knee osteoarthritis rehabilitation.
abstract: Wearable inertial sensors enable repeated movement recording during knee osteoarthritis rehabilitation, but methods for summarizing multivariable changes across routine sessions remain exploratory. This retrospective technical evaluation examined a normalized transport-derived deviation (NTD) constructed from paired shank-mounted inertial measurement units. Seven participants contributed 46 paired-sensor sessions over 45 d. An approximately 30 s active movement segment from each session was divided into 13 windows and represented using 58 time-domain, frequency-domain and cross-sensor features. Session distributions were compared with each participant's first usable sensor session using an archived entropically regularized transport implementation. The output was normalized by the baseline-to-final-session value. Mean NTD values at the scheduled assessment days were 0.00, 0.02, 0.23, 0.63 and 1.00. 14 of the 46 displayed values were structurally constrained baseline or final values; no monotonic constraint was applied to the 32 interior observations, which formed non-decreasing trajectories. At interior scheduled days 5, 15 and 30, absolute differences between mean NTD and participant-adjusted normalized elapsed time were 0.057, 0.076 and 0.019. 21 of the 46 archived calculations reached the 500-iteration limit without meeting the 1 × 10-6residual criterion. A log-domain stabilized recomputation of all 46 primary comparisons satisfied a 1 × 10-8criterion, with a mean absolute archived-to-stabilized NTD difference of 0.004 (maximum 0.018) across the 32 interior observations. Across support-point counts of 100-1000, interior archived NTD values changed by 0.009-0.026 on average. Routine paired-shank recordings were organized into ordered longitudinal trajectories and the resulting trajectory structure was numerically reproducible under the evaluated implementation. NTD should presently be interpreted as an implementation-specific retrospective coordinate rather than a validated rehabilitation outcome. By defining the requirements for standardized movement tasks, prospective normalization and reproducible sensor placement, these findings provide a practical foundation for prospective validation of transport-based rehabilitation assessment.

title: An Intensified Training Period Reduces REM Sleep but this Decline Can Be Mitigated by Ketone Ester Supplementation.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: We previously showed that a strenuous training day disrupts sleep efficiency and REM sleep, and that these disturbances can be counteracted by ketone monoester (R)-3-hydroxybutyl-(R)-3-hydroxybutyrate (KE) supplementation. However, the impact of prolonged intensified training on sleep quality, as well as the potential modulating effect of KE are unknown.
METHODS: We performed a double-blind study in which twenty-four trained male athletes completed a 7-week training program with a gradual increase in training load while receiving either 25g of a control drink (CON, n=12) or 25g of KE (n=12) after each training session and 30 minutes before sleep. At the start (PRE), week 3 (MID), and the end (POST) of the training program, we evaluated sleep using polysomnography, and perceived stress/recovery balance using the REST-Q questionnaire. Timing, duration, and relative intensity of exercise on each testing day were identical.
RESULTS: The progressive increase in training load induced a decrease in the perceived stress-recovery state in both groups (PRE: 73±21 vs. POST: 40±37, p<0.001, Hedges' g = 1.097). From PRE to MID, sleep efficiency improved by 3% in both groups (p=0.003, Hedges' g = 0.663) while wakefulness after sleep onset reduced by 2% (p=0.031, Hedges' g = 0.716). However, from PRE to POST, total REM sleep decreased by 2% in CON but increased by 3% in KE (p=0.002, for KE vs. CON, Hedges' g = 0.939). Perceived sleep quality did not differ between groups throughout the intervention.
CONCLUSIONS: Our data indicate that KE supplementation did not enhance the beneficial effect of an initial increase in training load on sleep but prevented the decline in REM sleep upon a further training load increment.

title: Central and peripheral vascular recovery following resistance exercise with and without blood flow restriction across age groups: a parallel group crossover randomized trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: High-intensity resistance training (HIRT) benefits musculoskeletal and vascular health but may be poorly tolerated by older adults. Low-intensity resistance training (LIRT) is an alternative, yet evidence on arterial stiffness is mixed, and it often fails to improve vascular health due to insufficient stimulus. Blood flow restriction (BFR) enhances hemodynamic stimulus, but its acute cardiovascular effects in older adults remain unclear.
PURPOSE: To compare central and peripheral vascular responses following acute LIRT with BFR versus HIRT across age groups.
METHODS: In a randomized crossover design, 19 young (22±3 years) and 19 older (70±9 years) adults completed three sessions: HIRT (3 × 10 reps at 75%1RM), LIRT+BFR (4 × 20 reps at 30%1RM with continuous cuff occlusion), and no exercise. Central and peripheral vascular function were assessed via oscillometric pulse wave analysis at rest, 5-min (RECOV1), and 30-min (RECOV2) post-exercise.
RESULTS: In older adults, neither HIRT nor LIRT+BFR altered total peripheral resistance (TPR), aortic reservoir function, or subendocardial viability ratio (SEVR) throughout post-exercise, with no differences observed between conditions. Conversely, young adults exhibited reductions at RECOV1 following HIRT in TPR (Δ = - 0.176 PRU), reservoir function (Δ = - 11.9%), and SEVR (Δ = - 47.1%), persisting at RECOV2 (all p < 0.05). LIRT+BFR elicited minor changes. Most variables normalized within 30 min for both groups.
CONCLUSION: In older adults, LIRT+BFR elicits post acute central vascular responses comparable to HIRT, with stable coronary perfusion and rapid recovery supporting the short-term tolerability of both modalities. LIRT+BFR thus represents a viable alternative to HIRT for older population.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov (ID: NCT06596304).

title: Error Related Negativity and Error Positivity: Neural Indices of Double-Faults in Elite Athletes.
abstract: ObjectiveError-related negativity (ERN) and error positivity (Pe) are key neural responses of human error monitoring. However, their relationship to behavioral adjustments after the mistakes in speeded laboratory experiments has shown mixed results. The present study examined whether ERN and Pe amplitudes would be better predictors of performance recovery following an error in a sport context than in a speeded laboratory task.MethodsFifteen male professional basketball players (18-26 years) performed a letter-based Eriksen Flanker task while their brain activity was recorded using 32-channel electroencephalography (EEG). Then, they completed a standardized 100-shot free-throw protocol on their home court. Recovery in the laboratory was measured as the ratio of back-to-back errors to total errors in the Flanker task, while recovery on the court was measured as the ratio of consecutive missed free throws to total misses. Pearson correlations and linear regression analysis were used to examine how ERP magnitudes relate to each recovery measure.ResultsAlthough ERN and Pe amplitudes were not associated with the laboratory consecutive-error ratio (all p values >.05), they were significant predictors of the field consecutive-miss ratio. Athletes with larger Pe and ERN amplitudes had significantly fewer consecutive misses (p < .001 and p = .017).ConclusionsERN and Pe may be less relevant for predicting specific post-error adjustments to immediate task demands and more relevant for predicting overall regulatory capacity in ecologically valid settings. Our findings highlight the need to use real-world performance measures when linking error monitoring with the realm of athletic performance.

title: Association of sleep efficiency with cardiac autonomic modulation in young and professional soccer players during pre-season.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study investigated the association between sleep efficiency and cardiac autonomic modulation in young and professional soccer players during pre-season.
METHODS: A cross-sectional quantitative study was conducted with 53 male soccer players divided into three categories: U-15 (n = 12), U-17 (n = 15), and professionals (n = 26). Sleep quality was assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), cardiac autonomic modulation via heart rate variability (HRV) recorded by a 10-lead electrocardiograph and analyzed with Kubios HRV 2.0, and cardiorespiratory capacity estimated through the Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test. Body composition was assessed by tetrapolar electrical bioimpedance. Statistical analyses included one-way ANOVA, Welch's ANOVA, chi-square and Fisher's exact tests, Pearson correlation, and simple linear regression, with significance set at p < 0.05.
RESULTS: Professional athletes demonstrated significantly higher VO₂max (50.5 ± 4.56 ml·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹; p < 0.001), lower resting heart rate (54.9 ± 8.65 bpm; p = 0.03), and greater parasympathetic modulation (RMSSD: 82.8 ± 17.5 ms; p < 0.001) compared to youth categories. Sleep efficiency was significantly higher in professionals (90.7 ± 6.13%; p = 0.01) and positively correlated with RMSSD. A significant association was found between RMSSD levels and global sleep quality (p = 0.004; X² = 0.50), as well as between RMSSD and VO₂max classification (p = 0.01; X² = 0.40).
CONCLUSION: Sleep efficiency is positively associated with cardiac autonomic modulation and aerobic performance in soccer players. While the superior physiological profile of professionals reflects a synergy between training adaptations and biological maturation, HRV and PSQI constitute complementary monitoring tools for integrated athlete assessment across competitive categories.

title: Improving sleep monitoring in athletes: a comparative evaluation of four automated sleep scoring algorithms on 204 polysomnography recordings.
abstract: ObjectiveWith advancements in AI, automated sleep scoring offers the potential for fast, precise, and cost-effective analysis. This study aimed to evaluate the accuracy, robustness, and clinical agreement of four algorithms compared to manual PSG in athletes to determine their suitability for real-life use.ApproachData from 75 athletes (204 polysomnography recordings) were retrospectively collected from studies conducted in our laboratory. Manual scoring was compared to four automated sleep staging algorithms: Luna, U-Sleep, YASA, and GSSC. Performance was evaluated based on accuracy (per stage, macro and weighted F1), sensitivity (confusion matrices), robustness (signal quality: R 2 ; individual differences: beta coefficients) and clinical relevance (prediction of total sleep time, sleep onset latency and wake after sleep onset).Main resultsAll algorithms demonstrated strong agreement with manual scoring, with macro F1 scores of 0.76 (GSSC), 0.71 (U-Sleep), 0.70 (YASA), and 0.69 (Luna). GSSC was the most accurate and robust across sport, physiological, behavioral, and anthropometric variables. It also reliably predicted total sleep time, sleep onset latency and wake after sleep onset, showing minimal bias and narrow limits of agreement. GSSC and Luna were the most resilient to signal degradation (R² = 0.08), compared to YASA (R² = 0.16) and U-Sleep (R² = 0.29).SignificanceAutomated sleep staging algorithms demonstrated accuracy comparable to typical inter-rater agreement, supporting their broader use in athletes. GSSC emerged as the most accurate and robust option, particularly resilient to signal quality degradation, a common challenge in ecological sport settings. By reducing scoring time and removing the need for expert raters, these algorithms could make polysomnography more accessible for both routine sleep monitoring and large-scale research, enabling more individualized recovery strategies and deeper insights into how sleep architecture influences athletic performance.

title: Combined anterior cruciate ligament and anterolateral ligament reconstruction leads to better postural control than isolated anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction in the early postoperative phase.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Recent studies suggest that the anterolateral ligament (ALL) contributes to knee rotational stability by acting synergistically with the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). Although combined ACL and ALL reconstruction has shown benefits in physical examination, subjective physical scales, and return-to-sport or re-rupture rates, few studies have compared postural control. This study aimed to compare postural control between isolated ACL reconstruction and combined ACL and ALL reconstruction.
METHODS: Between June 2016 and July 2022, patients who underwent isolated ACL reconstruction (n = 37) or combined ACL and ALL reconstruction (n = 30) were included. Static and dynamic postural control were assessed using the Biodex Balance System and the Y-balance test (YBT) preoperatively and at three and six months postoperatively.
FINDINGS: A total of 67 patients were enrolled, including 49 men and 18 women, with a mean age of 30.2 ± 8.1 years and a mean body mass index of 25.98 ± 3.6 kg/m2. In the YBT, which assesses dynamic postural control as the contralateral limb moves away from the center of gravity, significant main effects of time and group were observed, except in the anterior direction. The YBT-posteromedial (p = 0.009) and YBT-posterolateral (p = 0.049) directions, which reflect knee rotational stability, was significantly better in the combined ACL and ALL reconstruction group than in the isolated ACL reconstruction group.
INTERPRETATION: At three months postoperatively, combined ACL and ALL reconstruction showed better dynamic postural control than isolated ACL reconstruction, particularly during tasks requiring multidirectional postural adjustments.

title: Cardiac autonomic and hemodynamic responses to two-stage cycling and post-exercise recovery with partial blood flow restriction in young males.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This study compared acute cardiovascular and cardiac autonomic responses during graded (two-stage) aerobic cycling and subsequent recovery performed with and without partial blood flow restriction (BFR).
METHODS: Fifteen young males completed two sessions in a crossover design (control vs. bilateral thigh BFR). Each session included rest, 5 min of cycling at 40% maximal power output (Pmax), 5 min at 60% Pmax, and 10 min of recovery; BFR was released immediately at exercise cessation. ECG and arterial blood pressure were recorded. RR interval, mean arterial blood pressure (MBP), HRV (lnRMSSD, lnSDNN, HF, LF, LF/HF), and composite indices of cardiac sympathetic and parasympathetic activity (SNS, PNS) were derived from 3-min segments at rest, exercise, and recovery. Heart rate recovery at 30, 60, and 120 s after exercise cessation (HRR30, HRR60, HRR120) was calculated. Two-way repeated-measures ANOVA tested condition, time, and interaction.
RESULTS: Time × condition interactions were observed for RR interval (p=0.015) and MBP (p=0.003), indicating altered hemodynamic kinetics under BFR, primarily during recovery. HRV indices showed no time × condition interactions; however, BFR produced lower lnRMSSD, lnSDNN, HF, and PNS and higher SNS than control (all p<0.05), whereas LF and LF/HF were unchanged. HRR30 (p=0.040), HRR60 (p<0.001), and HRR120 (p=0.010) were attenuated under BFR.
CONCLUSIONS: BFR modifies cardiovascular regulation during two-stage cycling and recovery and induces sustained autonomic shifts toward reduced parasympathetic and increased sympathetic modulation, largely independent of exercise intensity. Altered recovery kinetics following cuff release highlight the importance of careful monitoring during the recovery phase when applying BFR.

title: The Sonographic Muscle Injury Classification in Soccer: proposal for an ultrasound-based muscle injury classification.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To propose a novel ultrasound-based classification system for muscle injuries in soccer players, termed the Sonographic Muscle Injury Classification in Soccer (SOMICS), and to evaluate its association, ordinal consistency, and agreement with the British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC).
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This was a cross-sectional observational study including 51 adolescent male soccer players (11-19 years of age) with suspected acute myotendinous injuries. All athletes underwent ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) within 24 h after injury. Four experienced radiologists, working independently, reviewed the images.
RESULTS: Interobserver agreement was substantial for ultrasound (κ = 0.65) and MRI (κ = 0.70). A strong ordinal correlation was observed between SOMICS and BAMIC categories (ρ = 0.80; p < 0.001), with a statistically significant association (χ2 = 52.53; p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: The SOMICS demonstrated significant association, ordinal consistency, and substantial agreement with the BAMIC for severity stratification of muscle injuries. Although not intended to replace MRI-based classifications for prognostic decision-making, the SOMICS provides a structured, reproducible ultrasound-based approach that may be useful in clinical settings where MRI is not readily available or as a first-line imaging tool.

title: Sleep Quality and Adherence to the Mediterranean Diet in Male Young Adults: An Exploratory Study Among Amateur Soccer Players, Physically Active Individuals, and Individuals with High Sitting Time.
abstract: Amateur soccer players represent a relatively understudied population and often combine training with study or work, facing daily challenges that can impact sleep, diet, and circadian-related behaviors. Since these factors are important for health, recovery, and well-being, this study aimed to examine sleep quality, adherence to the Mediterranean diet, and chronotype in amateur soccer players compared with physically active individuals and individuals with high sitting time. The sample comprised 55 male young adults (23.36 ± 3.11 years): amateur soccer players (n = 20), physically active individuals (n = 18), and individuals with high sitting time (n = 17). All participants completed the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), the PREvención con DIeta MEDiterránea (PREDIMED), and the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ). Group comparisons were performed using appropriate parametric or non-parametric tests, and exploratory correlation analyses were used to examine associations among sleep quality, Mediterranean diet adherence, and chronotype. Lower PSQI scores (p < 0.001) were observed in soccer players (3.80 ± 1.32) and physically active individuals (4.17 ± 1.92) than in individuals with high sitting time (6.24 ± 2.05). No significant between-group differences were found in PREDIMED (soccer players = 6.80 ± 2.22; physically active individuals = 7.50 ± 1.89; individuals with high sitting time = 7.29 ± 2.42) and MEQ (soccer players = 51.60 ± 5.90; physically active individuals = 50.89 ± 7.70; individuals with high sitting time = 51.82 ± 11.43). Exploratory correlation analyses, without correction for multiple testing, identified a negative association between MEQ and PSQI in individuals with high sitting time (r = -0.514, p = 0.035). These findings describe group differences in self-reported sleep quality, whereas Mediterranean diet adherence and chronotype appeared similar across groups.

title: Subperiosteal hematoma of the ilium in adolescent athletes with acute groin pain: clinical and MRI features of a radiograph-occult injury pattern.
abstract: Subperiosteal hematoma of the ilium is an uncommon MRI finding in young athletes with acute groin pain and is frequently occult on plain radiographs. This study aimed to characterize its clinical presentation, MRI findings, associated injuries, and return-to-sport outcomes. This retrospective single-center case series included athletes aged ≤22 years who underwent MRI for acute sports-related groin pain with negative or inconclusive radiographs between 2017 and 2025. Patients meeting predefined MRI criteria for subperiosteal hematoma of the ilium were identified, and clinical, imaging, and outcome data were analyzed descriptively. Twenty of 91 patients (22.0%) met the MRI criteria. Their mean age was 13.9 ± 1.5 years, 19 (95%) were male, and 18 (90%) had open physes. Periosteal elevation was present in all patients, and 19 (95%) demonstrated a predominantly subperiosteal fluid collection, most commonly with a lentiform configuration. Associated anterior inferior iliac spine avulsion injury or intramuscular iliacus injury was identified in 10 patients (50%). All patients were managed nonoperatively and returned to unrestricted sports participation after progressive rehabilitation at a mean of 4.5 ± 2.2 weeks. Subperiosteal hematoma of the ilium is a reproducible MRI finding in predominantly skeletally immature athletes with acute sports-related groin pain and negative or inconclusive radiographs. Recognition of periosteal elevation with a predominantly subperiosteal fluid collection may facilitate diagnosis of this radiograph-occult injury pattern. Although the underlying injury mechanism remains hypothetical, prospective studies are needed to clarify its clinical significance.

title: Female Versus Male Differences in Burnout With Sport: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
CONTEXT: Burnout is a widely recognized problem in sports. Female athletes have been found to experience more emotional exhaustion and less depersonalization, key components of burnout, than their male counterparts. Researchers have found varied results when comparing rates of burnout between male and female athletes.
OBJECTIVE: This study aims to review the current literature with the goal of determining what differences exist between male and female athletes regarding sport burnout.
DATA SOURCES: PubMed (Medline), Cochrane library, SPORTDiscus, CINAHL, Embase, and Web of Science.
STUDY SELECTION: Articles that were originally written in English, included athletes participating in organized sport, evaluated athletic burnout, and compared rates of burnout among different sexes were included in this review. Articles that were cadaveric, animal, review, or expert opinions were excluded.
STUDY DESIGN: Systematic review.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 4.
DATA EXTRACTION: The age, sex, sport, and level of athletic competition of individual athletes were extracted from each article in addition to burnout rates and outcome scores of male and female athletes.
RESULTS: Of the 18 studies included in this review, 10 (56%) found no significant differences in sport burnout among male and female athletes, 7 (39%) found that female athletes experienced greater burnout than male athletes and 1 (5.6%) found that male athletes experienced greater burnout than female athletes. Reduced sense of accomplishment and physical/emotional exhaustion were implicated in creating more burnout among female athletes than their male counterparts in 4 studies.
CONCLUSION: It remains unclear how the constructs of sex and gender affect athlete burnout. The heterogeneity of studies included in this review prevented the analysis of how participation in team sports, participation in individual sports, level of competition, and the coach-athlete relationship influence sport burnout. More standardized studies are needed to better evaluate the effect sex and gender have on athlete burnout as well as how athletes involved in various sports are affected by burnout.

title: Hitting Volume Demands during Men's Australian Open and Roland Garros: Effects of Tournament, Competition Phase, and Player Level.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hitting volume is a key component of external load in tennis, as it reflects the cumulative demands associated with the repetitive execution of complex stroke actions during match play. Despite its relevance for workload monitoring and injury prevention, limited information is available regarding how hitting volume demands vary according to playing surface, tournament progression, and player level in elite professional tennis.
HYPOTHESIS: Hitting volume demands vary according to tournament, competition phase, and player ranking level.
STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional observational study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: Match data were collected from 474 player-match observations (236 at the Australian Open and 238 at Roland Garros). Complete stroke count data were available for 384 player-match observations, comprising 214,874 analyzed strokes. Match duration, stroke counts, and rally length distributions were compared across tournaments, competition phases, and ranking groups.
RESULTS: Roland Garros matches were characterized by greater overall hitting volumes than Australian Open matches (P = 0.04), despite a similar number of points played. These differences were reflected in higher groundstroke volumes and a greater proportion of medium and long rallies at Roland Garro (P < 0.05). Competition phase was associated with differences in selected stroke-count variables and rally structure, with later-round matches showing a greater proportion of prolonged rallies (P < 0.05), although overall match duration and total stroke volume remained comparable. Differences according to player level were also identified. Top 10 players accumulated lower overall hitting volumes (P < 0.05) and exhibited a lower proportion of short rallies together with a greater proportion of prolonged exchanges than lower-ranked players (P < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: Hitting volume demands were associated with tournament, competition phase, and player ranking level. These contextual factors should be considered when interpreting competition loads and planning training and recovery strategies during Grand Slam competition.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The reported competition reference values may assist coaches and sports medicine practitioners in optimizing surface-specific training prescription, workload monitoring, fatigue management, and return-to-play strategies in professional tennis.

title: UEFA consensus guidelines on anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury in Women's football - part one: risk factors and prevention.
abstract: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries are among the most burdensome injuries in women's football, carrying significant consequences for players and the football community. To develop practical, evidence-based guidelines for ACL injury prevention, UEFA convened a multidisciplinary expert panel of 31 doctors, sports scientists, physiotherapists, and a player. Using the RAND-UCLA Appropriateness Method, 101 evidence statements were synthesised from existing literature and subjected to a modified Delphi process with three rounds of confidential voting. Consensus was reached on 88 statements. Through online and in-person discussions, this evidence was integrated with expert and clinical and practical judgement to produce actionable recommendations tailored to women's football. The guidelines conclude that ACL injuries in women's football typically occur in non-contact situations during high-intensity movements such as cutting, pressing, or landing, and may be influenced by a combination of modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors. Proposed modifiable factors include deficits in neuromuscular control, strength, and movement quality, which can be addressed through multicomponent prevention strategies. These programmes were identified as the most effective, incorporating plyometric, strength, and proximal control exercises performed two to three times per week for 15 to 20 minutes, with evidence showing they can reduce non-contact ACL injuries when adherence is high. Successful implementation requires context-specific tailoring, embedding programmes into routine training, and addressing barriers such as limited resources, time constraints, and lack of coach education. The guidelines recommend enhancing buy-in through co-creation with coaches and players, integrating prevention into existing practice, and strengthening organisational and policy support to sustain long-term adoption.

title: Biceps rerouting and derotational radial osteotomy: A technique for correcting forearm supination in NBPBP.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Forearm supination deformity is a recognized late sequela of neonatal brachial plexus birth palsy (NBPBP) that can impair functional positioning of the hand and limit activities requiring forearm pronation. Surgical options include forearm osteotomy, tendon rerouting, tendon transfer, and combined procedures. We describe a modified technique combining derotational radial osteotomy with biceps tendon rerouting using cortical button fixation.
METHODS: This was a single-patient technical case report. An 18-year-old male with longstanding fixed forearm supination deformity secondary to NBPBP underwent radial derotational osteotomy and biceps tendon rerouting. The biceps tendon was detached with the forearm in maximal supination, rerouted through the interosseous space, and secured with a cortical button with the forearm in maximal pronation. A radial osteotomy was subsequently performed toward pronation with approximately 30° to 45° of rotational correction. Postoperative rehabilitation included protected immobilization followed by progressive range of motion and strengthening.
RESULTS: Preoperatively, the forearm rested in approximately 15° of supination, with active pronation limited to neutral and active supination to approximately 50°. Following surgery, the forearm rested in approximately 15° to 20° of pronation. Passive forearm rotation improved from 45° of supination to 40° of pronation preoperatively to 60° of supination to 75° of pronation postoperatively. At 12 months, active pronation improved from neutral to 55° of pronation. No postoperative complications were reported during follow-up. The patient participated in occupational therapy 1 to 2 times weekly during recovery.
CONCLUSION: This case demonstrates the technical feasibility of combining radial derotational osteotomy with biceps tendon rerouting using cortical button fixation for longstanding supination deformity following NBPBP. The technique provides an additional fixation option for tendon rerouting while addressing the underlying osseous rotational deformity. Given the single-patient design and absence of comparative or biomechanical data, further study is required to determine whether cortical button fixation offers advantages over established tendon fixation methods and to evaluate the reproducibility and clinical efficacy of this approach.

title: ATG5-overexpressing MSCs improve ligament healing with an associated shift toward M2 macrophage polarization in aged rats.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Autophagy is crucial for maintaining mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) function, yet its role in age-related ligament healing deficits remains unclear. This study examined the relationship between MSC autophagic activity and age-related ligament healing and evaluated ATG5 overexpression effects on autophagy and regeneration.
METHODS: Medial collateral ligament (MCL) injury models were established in young and aged rats. Healing was assessed using ultrasound, histology, immunohistochemistry, apoptosis assays, and biomechanical testing. Aged MSCs were engineered to overexpress ATG5 and transplanted into injured ligaments. Repair outcomes and macrophage polarization changes were evaluated.
RESULTS: Aged rats exhibited impaired ligament healing, and aged MSCs displayed reduced autophagic activity. ATG5 overexpression enhanced autophagy in aged MSCs, and transplantation of ATG5-overexpressing MSCs was associated with improved ligament repair in aged rats, including increased proliferation, angiogenesis, collagen organization, and biomechanical strength, alongside reduced apoptosis. ATG5-overexpressing MSC transplantation was also associated with lower M1 and higher M2 macrophage markers and a more anti-inflammatory cytokine profile. Reduced MSC autophagy was associated with age-related ligament healing deficits.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings support a potential relationship among ATG5-associated autophagy, macrophage phenotype, and improved ligament repair, while the causal dependence of therapeutic effects on autophagy and macrophage polarization remains to be established.

title: More than fuel: Why athletes need better language around food.
abstract: "Food is fuel" is a widely used phrase in sport settings intended to emphasize the importance of nutrition for performance. While nutrition is essential for health and success, this framing may unintentionally reinforce a narrow, performance-oriented understanding of eating that has implications for athletes' relationships with food and their bodies. Athletes are at heightened risk for eating concerns, low energy availability, and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs), and aspects of sport culture may contribute to rigid, rule-based approaches to eating. This commentary argues that "food is fuel" language reflects and reinforced broader sports norms centered around optimization, control, and performance. Potential consequences include reduced attunement to internal cues and the moralization of food choices, particularly in sport environments where appearance and performance are closely intertwined. Language is proposed as a modifiable factor for prevention and more flexible, athlete-centered approaches to discussing food and eating are identified. Rather than dismissing the importance of nutrition in athletics, this commentary advocates for broader conceptualizations of eating that acknowledge its physical, psychological, social, and cultural functions and support athletes in developing sustainable relationships with food throughout and beyond their athletic careers.

title: Imaging of acute sports injuries of the shoulder girdle.
abstract: Acute injuries of the shoulder girdle commonly result from sports activities and lead to imaging studies. Radiologists who interpret these studies should be familiar with traumatic mechanisms and the imaging manifestations of glenohumeral dislocation, acromioclavicular sprain, rotator cuff tear, labral tear, osseous contusion or fracture, and myotendinous strain. Imaging findings are crucial for making accurate diagnoses, grading the severity of injuries, guiding treatment plans, and managing the athletes' expectations for rehabilitation and return to sport. In this review article, we address common and uncommon injuries in both young and mature athletes. Focusing on magnetic resonance imaging, we provide examples of classic injuries and discuss pitfalls that challenge diagnostic interpretation.

title: Advanced Footwear Technology in Distance Running: What We Know, What We Don't Know, and Future Directions.
abstract: Over the past decade, running shoes have undergone substantial innovation with the emergence of Advanced Footwear Technology (AFT). Shoes with AFT are typically characterized by highly compliant (deformable) and resilient (high energy return) midsole foams, embedded curved stiffening elements, low mass, and a rockered longitudinal geometry. This expert statement aims to synthesize established knowledge, remaining uncertainties and key directions for future research on AFT in middle- and long-distance running. Current literature demonstrates robust improvements in running economy and performance with AFT, with reported metabolic savings of approximately 2%-4%, and corresponding performance improvements of 1%-3%. These benefits likely arise from a combination of "acute" and possibly "long-term" mechanisms. Proposed acute mechanisms include decreased muscle force production due to higher positive work from energy-returning foams, lower muscle force production to accommodate mechanical running demands due to compliant midsoles, and improved mechanical efficiency associated with greater longitudinal bending stiffness and curved geometry. Importantly, AFT features have a synergistic effect, with the relative importance of each mechanism differing depending on the context. Emerging evidence also suggests potential reductions in muscle damage/inflammation and soreness, which could support better physiological resilience, and higher training volumes/quality. From a biomechanical injury risk perspective, AFT can redistribute loading, potentially increasing metatarsal and tarsal stress while reducing tibia and possibly Achilles tendon loading. However, injury risk associated with AFT use remains equivocal, with limited high-quality data. Notably, substantial inter-individual variability has been observed, influencing both running economy and potential injury risk although the determinants of this variability remain unclear.

title: Wearable Technologies and Artificial Intelligence in Sports Medicine: A Systematic Narrative Review of Injury Prevention and Rehabilitation.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Wearable technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) are shifting sports medicine from episodic, subjective assessment toward continuous, data-driven injury surveillance. This review aimed to map the main wearable sensor modalities used in injury prevention and rehabilitation, evaluate AI architectures applied to biomechanical and physiological data, summarize clinically relevant applications by anatomical region, and identify methodological, ethical, and implementation challenges.
METHODS: A systematic narrative review was conducted across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for studies published from 2016 to 2026, supplemented by manual reference screening. Search terms combined wearable sensors, AI and machine learning, and sports medicine outcomes. After title and abstract screening of 614 records and full-text assessment of 87 articles, 28 studies met the inclusion criteria.
RESULTS: Inertial measurement units, GPS/GNSS, surface electromyography, and photoplethysmography were the most frequently reported sensor modalities. Deep learning, ensemble methods, and multimodal fusion were commonly used to process biomechanical and physiological signals. One hybrid IMU-sEMG study involving 50 athletes reported 92.3% accuracy, 90.5% recall, and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.93 for classifying biomechanical injury-risk states. An ankle-monitoring study using data from 87 athletes across 12 sports reported 87.4% overall detection accuracy, a 12.1% false-alarm rate, and 17.2 ms latency. However, substantial heterogeneity in study design, populations, outcomes, and validation methods prevented direct comparison or pooled quantitative interpretation.
CONCLUSION: Wearable-AI systems show promising potential for injury-risk monitoring, rehabilitation, and return-to-play support. Wider clinical adoption will require more diverse populations, longitudinal and field-based validation, improved model interpretability, standardized protocols, and robust ethical, legal, and governance frameworks.

title: Editorial Commentary: Want to Try Anterior Cruciate Ligament Repair? Maximize Your Chances of Success by Choosing the Right Anterior Cruciate Ligaments to Repair Rather Than Reconstruct.
abstract: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) repair represents an attractive choice for certain patients because of a higher rate of return to sport as well as a potentially faster recovery time. Recent evidence has shown that younger age and synovial sheath integrity <50% are associated with increased risk of failure after arthroscopic ACL repair. This makes sense because the synovial sheath is responsible for providing blood supply and proprioceptive nerve endings to the ACL, as well as protection of the ligament from the degradative environment of synovial fluid. As with any procedure, indications are refined over time based on new evidence. Although I believe that ACL reconstruction will remain the gold standard for the treatment of ACL tears, I also believe that our rates of success with ACL repair will improve as indications are further refined over time.

title: Running-based rehabilitation does not improve muscle function after volumetric muscle loss despite improving hindlimb weight-bearing asymmetry in mice.
abstract: Volumetric muscle loss (VML) is a traumatic skeletal muscle injury characterized by chronic functional impairments in the affected muscle and adjacent uninjured bone. Rehabilitative strategies aimed at restoring limb function following VML, including voluntary running, have shown limited efficacy and in some cases have been detrimental. One potential explanation is disproportional loading of the uninjured contralateral limb during running, but evaluation of unilateral weight-bearing following VML has not been explored. This study was designed to evaluate if the limited response to rehabilitation following VML could be explained by limb loading asymmetry. Twelve-week-old C57Bl/6J mice (n = 24; equal males/females) were randomized to three groups: Naïve-Run, VML, and VML-Run. Two weeks post-VML, mice in running groups were provided free access to wheels for 6 weeks. Weight-bearing asymmetry was assessed before injury and biweekly thereafter. Terminally at ∼20 weeks of age, in vivo muscle function was evaluated, and muscles and bones were saved for analyses. Prior to injury, no difference in weight-bearing asymmetry was observed across groups. VML-injured mice exhibited similar weight-bearing asymmetries prior to running. Following 6 weeks of running, VML-Run mice regained weight-bearing symmetry comparable to Naïve-Run. Despite this, remaining muscle function remained persistently impaired following VML injury. Collectively this works suggests that voluntary running promotes favourable weight-bearing adaptations following VML, but does not improve muscle function or the mechanical properties of the adjacent bone.

title: Effects of anti-aging diets and exercise on age-related musculoskeletal diseases via gut microbiota modulation.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: This review summarizes evidence on how anti-aging diets and exercise influence age-related musculoskeletal diseases through modulation of the gut microbiota. With population aging, these diseases are public health concerns. The gut microbiota regulates bone, joint, and muscle health via the gut‑joint, gut‑bone, and gut‑muscle axis. Few reviews integrate diet-exercise synergy with mechanistic pathways linking microbial changes to tissue outcomes.
DISCUSSION: Anti‑aging dietary strategies, classified into caloric restriction (ketogenic diet, fasting‑mimicking diet, intermittent fasting, time‑restricted feeding) and isocaloric nutrient restriction (e.g. protein or amino acid restriction), reshape gut microbiota composition and function. Caloric restriction and intermittent fasting reduce inflammation and benefit joint and muscle health, whereas long‑term ketogenic or protein/amino acid restriction may adversely affect bone density and muscle anabolism. Moderate exercise increases microbial diversity, enriches beneficial taxa (Akkermansia, Bifidobacterium), and boosts short‑chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, especially butyrate. Exercise also strengthens intestinal barrier integrity, reduces lipopolysaccharide (LPS)‑induced systemic inflammation, and alleviates osteoarthritis (OA), bone loss, and sarcopenia in preclinical models. Combined diet and exercise may provide greater benefits than either alone. However, most evidence derives from animal or small human studies, and causality remains unclear. Future research should clarify causal mechanisms via multi‑omics and germ‑free models.
CONCLUSION: This review suggests that both anti-aging diets and moderate exercise may improve age-related musculoskeletal diseases partly through gut microbiota modulation. Given substantial inter‑individual variability, future research should prioritize personalized nutrition and exercise prescriptions tailored to microbiota, genetic background, and lifestyle. These findings inform precision strategies to promote healthy aging.

title: Culturally Embedded Participation Restrictions in Indian Adults With Knee Osteoarthritis: An ICF-Based Qualitative Study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To identify culturally relevant functioning issues experienced by Indian adults with knee osteoarthritis (KOA) using the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) framework.
METHODS: A qualitative descriptive study using semi-structured focus group interviews was conducted with 38 ambulatory adults (35-85 years) diagnosed with knee osteoarthritis (KOA). Participants were recruited from physiotherapy outpatient departments and community settings using maximum variation sampling. Interviews were conducted in Gujarati, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, translated into English and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Meaningful concepts were systematically linked to ICF categories using established linking rules. Dual independent coding and consensus discussions ensured the analytic rigour.
RESULTS: This study included 38 participants with KOA. Fifty-five meaningful second-level categories were identified. The most represented components were activities and participation (41.2%) and body functions (29.4%). Frequently mapped first-level categories included mobility (n = 22), neuromusculoskeletal and movement-related functions (n = 9), d6 domestic life (n = 10), community, social and civic life (n = 7) and products and technology (n = 9). Sixteen additional categories not represented in the existing ICF Core Set for OA emerged, particularly relating to culturally embedded activities such as floor sitting, squatting for toileting and religious participation. Environmental barriers, including inaccessible infrastructure and limited rehabilitation services, influenced disability experience.
CONCLUSION: Functioning among Indian adults with KOA is influenced by culturally embedded participation demands and contextual barriers that are insufficiently captured in the existing ICF Core Set for osteoarthritis (OA). These findings provide preliminary empirical support for contextual validation of the ICF Core Set for OA and inform potential culturally responsive adaptation for KOA.

title: Anatomic feasibility of using Shark Screw tendon for humeral ligament re-construction in medial and posterolateral elbow instability.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Medial and posterolateral rotational instability of the elbow, often resulting from collateral ligament insufficiency, can lead to pain and functional impairment. Surgical re-construction is indicated when conservative treatment fails, yet complications such as graft failure and donor-site morbidity persist. This study investigates the anatomic and biomechanical feasibility of the Shark Screw tendon as a representative human allogeneic bone screw for humeral ligament fixation in cases of elbow instability.
METHODS: Eight fresh-frozen cadaveric specimens were used to evaluate the feasibility of the use of a Shark Screw tendon for humeral fixation on both medial and lateral sides. Cyclic loading and failure testing were performed to assess time-zero fixation characteristics and failure load.
RESULTS: A total of sixteen testing scenarios were conducted on the specimens. Implantation was technically feasible without anatomic limitations related to implant size or positioning. Six graft failures occurred (38%), all attributable to poor tissue quality. Tendon slippage was observed in 9 of 16 cases (56%) under progressively increasing axial load, while the Shark Screw tendon remained seated. The mean failure load was 101 N (±50) for medial insertions, 118 N (±77) for lateral insertions, and 110 N (±64) overall. After 100 cycles, tendon displacement averaged 1.1 mm (±0.4) during extension-flexion on the medial side, 1.0 mm (±1.0) on the lateral side, and 1.0 mm (±0.7) overall. During supination-pronation, displacement was 0.8 mm (±0.7) medially, 1.0 mm (±0.8) laterally, and 0.9 mm (±0.7) overall. No anchor pullout was observed, although one anchor tip fractured during insertion.
CONCLUSION: The Shark Screw tendon appears to be a feasible biologically integrative alternative for humeral fixation in medial and posterolateral elbow ligament re-construction, demonstrating preliminary time-zero fixation characteristics in a cadaveric model. Further biomechanical and clinical studies are needed to confirm long-term outcomes.

title: From donor programming to therapeutic performance: An evidence-calibrated narrative review of dental mesenchymal stromal/stem cell-derived extracellular vesicle preparations in oral and maxillofacial regeneration.
abstract: Dental mesenchymal stromal/stem cell-derived extracellular vesicle preparations are being investigated as cell-free interventions for oral and maxillofacial regeneration, but the evidence is heterogeneous in donor state, product identity, delivery context and endpoint level. This critical narrative review separates mechanistic confidence from translational readiness. Representative studies are mapped across dental pulp, periodontal ligament, deciduous-tooth, dental follicle, apical-papilla and gingival sources, while conditioned medium, secretome, small extracellular vesicle preparations, author-labelled exosome preparations, combined carrier-drug interventions and apoptotic vesicle preparations are kept distinct. The synthesis indicates that donor programming can yield directionally different outcomes across study-specific contexts; carrier-associated structural outcomes cannot automatically be assigned to a particle preparation; and molecular, histological and imaging outcomes do not establish durable organ function. Translation requires defined identity and purity, justified dose normalization, potency, batch comparability, stability, exposure, safety, manufacturing controls and indication-matched functional testing.

title: Emerging therapies for knee osteoarthritis.
abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is the most prevalent form of OA and a leading cause of chronic pain and disability worldwide. Its growing burden, driven mainly by ageing and obesity, is associated with major societal costs and increased cardiovascular mortality. Knee OA is now recognized as a heterogeneous whole-joint disease involving biomechanical, metabolic, inflammatory, osteochondral and neurovascular mechanisms. This complexity helps to explain why existing analgesics have modest efficacy and why disease-modifying OA drug development has repeatedly faltered. The therapeutic landscape is nevertheless evolving rapidly. Emerging symptomatic strategies include incretin-based therapies (semaglutide is the first to show substantial benefits for pain and function), neurotrophin modulation, extended-release intra-articular glucocorticoids, lubricating injectables and image-guided neurovascular interventions. In parallel, candidate disease-modifying OA drugs target cartilage anabolism, Wnt signalling, matrix-degrading enzymes, subchondral bone remodelling, immunometabolic pathways and local gene therapy. Several treatments, including locally administered GLP1 receptor agonists, the anabolic agent TPX-100 and intra-articular IL-1 receptor antagonist gene therapy, have shown encouraging signals, whereas mesenchymal stromal cell therapies have thus far demonstrated inconsistent efficacy across phase III clinical trials, highlighting the need for further standardization of mesenchymal stromal cell products and optimization of patient selection. Recent advances signal a shift towards a more diverse therapeutic landscape for knee OA, with emerging opportunities to target both symptoms and the underlying mechanisms of disease.

title: Small extracellular vesicles in osteoarthritis: A double‑edged sword regulating inflammation and cartilage homeostasis (Review).
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a progressive degenerative joint disease and a leading cause of pain, disability and loss of joint function in older adults worldwide. Small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) are small vesicles secreted by cells and found in various body fluids. They carry a range of bioactive molecules, including nucleic acids, proteins and lipids, and participate in numerous cellular physiological activities, such as cell death, inflammation, immunity, proliferation, migration and differentiation. Depending on their cellular origin, sEVs can exert opposing effects on OA: They may either aggravate inflammation and cartilage damage or suppress inflammation and promote cartilage repair. Therefore, this review focuses on the preclinical research evidence regarding the dual mechanism of 'promoting or treating' by sEVs in the disease of OA, aiming to construct a theoretical framework to provide a theoretical basis for the development and translational application of OA treatment strategies based on sEVs.

title: Imaging of Pediatric Hip Disorders in the Young Athlete.
abstract: Pediatric hip pain in young athletes encompasses a wide range of disorders related to skeletal immaturity and increasing athletic demands. Timely and accurate diagnosis is important, as delayed recognition may result in growth disturbances, instability, and long-term morbidity. Imaging plays a central role in differentiating clinically significant abnormalities from normal developmental variation and less consequential conditions. This review presents a pattern-based framework for evaluating pediatric hip pathology, organized into key categories based on dominant imaging patterns. Emphasis is placed on imaging findings that influence management and return-to-play decisions, including high-risk features and common pitfalls related to skeletal maturation. This approach provides a practical framework for diagnosis, risk stratification, and effective multidisciplinary communication.

title: Cannabigerol Enhances Muscle Strength and Performance in Dexamethasone-Treated Mice.
abstract: Sarcopenia is a major clinical condition associated with aging and is characterized by progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass and function. Resistance training is an effective intervention to counteract muscle atrophy; however, strategies that selectively enhance functional performance remain limited. Cannabigerol, a phytocannabinoid that is not a CB1 receptor agonist and therefore lacks psychotomimetic activity, has emerged as a potential modulator of neuromuscular function, although its role in skeletal muscle adaptation remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the effects of resistance exercise and cannabigerol, alone and in combination, in a dexamethasone-induced model of muscle atrophy in mice. Animals received dexamethasone (20 mg/kg, i.p.) for 12 days and were subsequently subjected to a 4-week ladder-based resistance exercise protocol. Cannabigerol (10 mg/kg, i.p.) was administered on training days. Resistance exercise restored muscle morphology and improved fatigue resistance. In contrast, cannabigerol acted mainly on neuromuscular performance, increasing muscle power while producing only a small increase in fiber cross-sectional area. Cannabigerol potentiated training-induced power output, increasing performance by ∼55% in the first week and up to ∼87% after 4 weeks compared to exercise alone. In addition, cannabigerol increased peak grip strength (∼10%) and lowered post-exercise blood lactate in sedentary animals (∼48%). These findings show that resistance exercise and cannabigerol exert complementary effects on skeletal muscleexercise promoting structural recovery and cannabigerol enhancing neuromuscular performance and lowering post-exercise lactateand support further investigation of cannabigerol as an adjunct to exercise in glucocorticoid-induced muscle atrophy.

title: Running on Empty: Relative Energy Deficiency in a Military Endurance Athlete.
abstract: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sports (RED-S) is a clinical syndrome characterized by low caloric intake relative to energy expenditure, resulting in a cascade of endocrine, metabolic, and musculoskeletal consequences. In females, hallmark features include decreased bone mineral density and menstrual dysfunction, though the syndrome affects multiple organ systems in both sexes. We present the case of a 22-year-old active-duty military member who suffered recurrent stress fractures, irregular menstrual cycles, and chronic fatigue that impacted her duty status. She was noted to have a long history of non-intentional calorie restriction and was eventually diagnosed with RED-S. Treatment consisted of a multidisciplinary approach, resulting in objective improvement in bone density and a successful return to full duty status. This case highlights the importance of early diagnosis and appropriate treatment of RED-S among military members to decrease morbidity and prevent limitations to military readiness and career progression.

title: Music-based emotional regulation and nutrition strategies for mental health support among medical student-athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Medical student-athletes face combined academic, clinical, and competitive training demands that may disrupt sleep, dietary routines, emotional regulation, recovery, and cognitive functioning.
OBJECTIVE: To examine associations between naturally occurring music-based emotional regulation, self-selected nutrition routines, psychophysiological recovery, and mental health-related markers using a non-interventional multimodal digital phenotyping framework.
METHODS: Over 8 weeks, 120 medical student-athletes were monitored without prescribed music, diet, therapy, or behavioral intervention. Data included wearable-derived nocturnal heart-rate variability, resting heart rate, sleep-wake rhythm, activity and training load, participant-recorded music use, meal timing, hydration routines, food-photo logs, and brief emotional reflections. Three indices were constructed: The Music Regulation Pattern Index, Nutrition Rhythm Stability Index, and Psychophysiological Recovery Balance Index.
RESULTS: Monitoring feasibility was high and index reliability was acceptable. Music-regulation patterns were more strongly associated with emotional balance and focus-related language, whereas nutrition-rhythm stability was more closely associated with sleep regularity, heart-rate variability stability, and recovery balance.
CONCLUSION: Naturally occurring music-use and nutrition-rhythm behaviors showed distinct associations with emotional and physiological recovery markers. Multimodal digital phenotyping may help identify potentially protective lifestyle patterns in medical student-athletes while preserving an observational, non-causal interpretation and avoiding unsupported treatment claims.

title: The effect of positive emotions on psychophysiological recovery and performance in athletes - investigating the undoing-hypothesis.
abstract: Athletes have to cope with psychosocial and physiological stressors, requiring recovery to ensure subsequent performance. According to the undoing-hypothesis, positive emotions (PE) may enhance psychophysiological recovery. The present two studies investigated the undoing hypothesis and its benefits for athletes' cognitive (Study 1; n = 60) and motor (Study 2; n = 30) performance. After a combined psychosocial-physiological stressor, participants either completed a five-minute PE induction (music; imagination exercise) or were assigned to a resting condition. Emotions, perceived stress-recovery, and physiological parameters (e.g., heart rate, heart rate variability, cortisol) were assessed. In Study 1, inhibition and cognitive flexibility were measured once. In Study 2, hand force and jump height were measured using a pre-posttest design. Due to the lack of psychological stress responses and successful PE induction, no conclusions could be drawn regarding the undoing hypothesis. Nevertheless, the present study provides valuable methodological insights into the challenges of testing the undoing hypothesis in athletes. These insights can inform the design and implementation of future studies and thereby contribute to advancing research on the undoing hypothesis in athletic populations.

title: Micro-recovery dosing in elite sport: an initiative-taking, organization-wide recovery framework.
abstract: Recovery in elite professional sport is now widely understood as a multidimensional process spanning physiological, psychological, cognitive, and social domains, yet recovery models applied in professional clubs and sporting organisations have been slow to reflect this. Most remain reactive and athlete-centred, leaving the full complexity of competitive fatigue inadequately addressed and the equivalent recovery demands on coaching and performance staff entirely unrecognised. No structural framework currently places initiative-taking, calendar-embedded multidimensional recovery as a deliberate component of seasonal planning. Main body. We introduce micro-recovery dosing (MRD): proactively planned, pre-scheduled 36-hour multidimensional recovery periods embedded within the competitive season as a proposed starting point at five to eight instances per year, extending to all members of the high-performance organisation. Drawing on neuromuscular recovery kinetics, autonomic science, sleep architecture research, occupational recovery psychology, and complex systems theory, we construct a convergent theoretical rationale for the proposed parameters and distinguish MRD from related constructs. We present a role-differentiated implementation framework with supporting evidence and a discussion of emerging AI-driven monitoring tools. Conclusions. Taken together, the four-domain convergent rationale and the complex systems perspective provide a theoretically coherent basis for MRD's proposed structure. We argue for a specific organisational transformation: the shift from recovery as an incidental gap between performance demands to an intentionally designed recovery architecture that encompasses athletes and staff alike. The article identifies the active ingredient problem as the central scientific challenge and sets out a structured empirical agenda.

title: Quantitative Muscle MRI Fat Fraction as a Biomarker of Disease Severity in Mitochondrial Myopathies.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Quantitative muscle MRI is increasingly used to assess structural muscle damage in inherited myopathies, but its application in primary mitochondrial myopathies (PMM) has not been systematically evaluated in large cohorts. Because PMM are clinically and genetically heterogeneous, objective imaging biomarkers are needed to quantify skeletal-muscle involvement and define meaningful subgroups. We assessed whether MRI-derived proton density fat fraction (PDFF) captures genotype- and phenotype-specific patterns of fatty replacement and reflects disease severity using motor function outcomes and circulating biomarkers.
METHODS: We performed a cross-sectional analysis of 49 adults with genetically confirmed PMM enrolled in a prospective natural history study. Participants underwent standardised lower-limb MRI, including T1-weighted sequences and mDIXON-QUANT fat fraction imaging. Muscle involvement was assessed semi-quantitatively with the modified Mercuri scale and quantitatively by PDFF measurement in selected pelvic girdle and thigh muscles. A total fat fraction score (FF sum) was calculated. PDFF was compared across genotypes and phenotypes and against MRC score, NSAA, 6-min walk test, 100-m run test, CK, serum creatinine, GDF15 and disease duration.
RESULTS: Mean age at onset was 26.3 ± 15.1 years, mean age at MRI was 50.0 ± 12.3 years, and median disease duration was 23 years (IQR 15-31). Genetic diagnoses included mtDNA variants in 29 patients (59.1%; single large-scale deletions, n = 19; point mutations, n = 10), nuclear variants in POLG (n = 8), TK2 (n = 8) and TWNK (n = 4). Phenotypes were exercise intolerance without overt weakness (n = 7), isolated progressive external ophthalmoplegia (PEO; n = 16), PEO-plus (n = 16) and progressive myopathy (n = 8). Highest median PDFF values were observed in tensor fasciae latae (31%), gluteus maximus (30%), sartorius (25%) and gracilis (20%). FF sum correlated with MRC score (r = -0.567, p < 0.0001), NSAA (r = -0.731, p < 0.0001), 100-m run test time (r = 0.629, p < 0.0001), 6-min walk distance (r = -0.311, p = 0.0476) and serum creatinine (r = -0.715, p < 0.0001), but not with CK or GDF15. TK2 deficiency showed the highest fat replacement, particularly in gluteus maximus and gracilis (p < 0.001). Progressive myopathy showed greater fatty replacement than other phenotypes (p < 0.001), while exercise intolerance showed higher fat fraction than isolated PEO (p = 0.033).
CONCLUSIONS: Quantitative muscle MRI provides objective and clinically meaningful measures of muscle involvement in PMM. MRI-derived fat fraction reflects disease severity, discriminates between genotypes and phenotypes, and detects subclinical muscle damage. These cross-sectional findings support PDFF as a candidate imaging biomarker for patient stratification and disease characterisation; prospective longitudinal studies will be required to establish its sensitivity to change and its validity as an outcome measure for therapeutic trials.

title: Biomimetic bilayer electrospun membrane simulating periodontal complex for orchestrated bone and fibrous tissue regeneration.
abstract: Guided tissue regeneration (GTR) is the core therapeutic strategy for repairing periodontal hard and soft tissue defects induced by periodontitis. Nevertheless, most current barrier membranes focus solely on alveolar bone reconstruction while ignoring the precise remodeling of the ordered periodontal ligament (PDL) microstructure, which impedes the integrated regeneration of functional periodontal tissues. To overcome these limitations, this study fabricated a novel bilayer composite GTR membrane with differentiated structural designs via sequential electrospinning for the synergistic and biomimetic regeneration of periodontal hard and soft tissues. The functionally graded membrane consisted of a dense, oriented poly-(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) nanofiber outer layer and a porous collagen inner layer incorporated with hydroxyapatite/β-tricalcium phosphate (HA/β-TCP) biphasic nanoparticles. The collagen matrix containing 60% HA and 40% β-TCP exhibited favorable mechanical properties that satisfy the mechanical requirements for periodontal repair. The dense PLGA layer effectively blocked the infiltration of human gingival fibroblasts (HGFs), and its physical barrier property could separate the external epithelial and connective tissues from the underlying bone tissue, offering a promising basis for the remodeling of periodontal hard and soft tissue. The inner Col/60% HA/40% β-TCP composite mimicked the natural organic-inorganic bone microenvironment and markedly promoted the adhesion, proliferation, and osteogenic differentiation of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells. The distinctive fibrous topography of the electrospun bilayer membrane provides contact guidance at the defect margins, facilitating the ordered regeneration and rearrangement of the periodontal ligament. In vivo rat periodontal defect experiments demonstrated that the bilayer membrane, compared with single-component membranes and commercial Bio-Gide membranes, significantly enhanced new bone formation and promoted the regeneration of ordered PDL-like fibrous structures with an orientation angle approaching that of the native periodontal ligament, achieving synchronized biomimetic regeneration of periodontal hard and soft tissues. In conclusion, this bilayer GTR membrane addresses the limited PDL reconstruction achieved by conventional barrier materials and provides a promising strategy for the targeted repair of complex periodontal defects.
