title: Evidence for the Effectiveness of the Performance Passport Within an Intelligence-Based Weightlifting Anti-Doping Programme.
abstract: Anti-doping organisations are tasked with detecting, deterring and preventing doping in sport, and because biological testing consumes a large share of budgets, efficient resource allocation is essential. Enhancing effectiveness requires better insight into how well current methods identify athletes at risk. The International Testing Agency (ITA) recently introduced the Athlete Performance Passport (APP), which uses competition performance data to flag at-risk weightlifters for targeted testing. This study evaluates the APP alongside established approaches, including Athlete Passport Management Unit (APMU) recommendations and atypical findings from the steroidal module of the Athlete Biological Passport (ABP). Data from 1960 male and 1583 female athletes were analysed, identifying 175 individuals (109 male and 66 female) who committed an Article 2.1 Anti-Doping Rule Violation (ADRV) between December 2009 and April 2025. The study assessed how effectively each method identified these athletes. Overall, the APP detected 34% of athletes who committed ADRVs during this period. Focusing on data since the steroidal passport's introduction in 2014, the APP identified 30% of ADRVs, outperforming APMU suspicious reports (17%) and atypical ABP steroidal profiles (10%). When combined, these methods identified 38% of ADRVs. These findings indicate that performance-based monitoring can strengthen anti-doping risk assessment and improve targeted testing strategies, particularly in sports with comprehensive competition data.

title: Bone biomarker and inflammatory cytokine responses to short-term low energy availability with and without preserved protein intake: a randomized, controlled, multi-period, cross-over trial.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Bone appears sensitive to low energy availability (LEA), with prolonged exposure linked to compromised bone health. Causality, however, along with underlying mechanisms, and the role of macronutrient availability remain unclear.
PURPOSE: To investigate the influence of short-term energy and protein manipulation on bone biomarker and inflammatory cytokine responses to acute exercise.
METHODS: Nineteen healthy, active young adults (9 females, 10 males) completed three 5-day dietary conditions in a randomized crossover design: adequate energy availability (AEA; 45 kcal·kgFFM·day-1), LEA (15 kcal·kgFFM·day-1) and LEA with protein matched to AEA (LEA-P). On days 1 and 5, participants completed a standardized exercise protocol comprising 45 min of cycling at 65% of pre-defined peak power output followed by a Wingate test, with blood samples collected at prespecified time-points to assess fasted and post-exercise bone biomarker and inflammatory cytokine responses.
RESULTS: Fasted P1NP was lower following both energy-restricted trials compared with AEA, and remained lower during post-exercise recovery following LEA-P. CTX-1 was higher in the post-exercise recovery period following LEA-P only. Multiple inflammatory cytokines (IL6, IL8, IL10, ILRa, and IL1β) increased at distinct time-points in both energy-restricted trials. Overall, evidence for condition effects relative to AEA was more consistent following LEA-P than LEA.
CONCLUSION: Short-term energy restriction suppressed biomarkers indicative of bone formation and augmented the inflammatory cytokine response to exercise, with some, but less consistent evidence for increased bone resorption. Preserving protein intake did not attenuate these effects. In contrast, this condition was associated with more consistent and pronounced perturbations, potentially reflecting reduced carbohydrate availability rather than protein per se.

title: Concussion symptom clusters and changes in symptom reporting and severity following multiple concussions in male professional rugby league players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Symptom reporting remains an important part of the diagnosis and management of concussion. Understanding the patterns of symptoms and symptom clusters in athletes with multiple concussions may be clinically valuable. The purpose of this study was to characterise acute symptom reporting in players with multiple concussions.
METHODS: National Rugby League (NRL) players who have sustained multiple concussions between the 2017 and 2022 seasons were included in the study. Data included the symptoms reported on the Sport Concussion Assessment Tool - 5th Edition (SCAT5) during the Head Injury Assessment by players who were subsequently diagnosed with concussion. K-means clustering with k = 6 centres was performed on symptom severity data. Each concussion episode was assigned to one symptom cluster based on the athlete's symptom presentation. Transitions between symptom clusters from initial to subsequent concussions were visualised using a Sankey plot.
RESULTS: There were 120 players who sustained more than one concussion, including 75 players with two, 23 with three, 15 with four, and 7 players with five or more medically diagnosed concussions. The average duration between concussions was 441 days (SD: 332; Md: 370; range: 11-1435 days). There were 6 different symptom clusters identified. Players were commonly found to transition between clusters for subsequent concussions, most commonly the 'Asymptomatic' cluster. There was no relationship found for days between concussions and symptom count or severity. Symptom severity, but not symptom count, was associated with days until medical clearance.
CONCLUSION: Acute symptom reporting varies with subsequent concussions, making it difficult to predict post-concussion symptoms in individual players. Acute symptom severity was associated with time to medical clearance, whereas the number of concussions in the preceding two years was not.

title: The role of plantar flexor function, isometric strength and task-specific kinetics, in sprint and jump performance.
abstract: The role of isometric plantar flexion (PF) strength in sprinting and jumping is unclear and, in part, may be due to methodological issues with isometric dynamometry leading to inaccurate measures of PF strength. In addition, the relationship, and thus functional relevance, of isometric PF strength with PF kinetics during these athletic tasks remains unknown. The aim of this study was to assess the interrelationships of isometric PF strength, task-specific sprint and jump PF kinetics and overall performance during jumps and sprint acceleration. Three-dimensional kinematics and ground reaction forces were recorded in 38 healthy individuals of varying athletic ability (18 females; height 1.75 ± 0.09 m; Mass: 70.9 ± 10.0 kg, Age 23 ± 3 years) during: standing isometric PF dynamometry, countermovement jumps (CMJ), drop jumps (DJ) and sprints. Isometric PF strength and sprint/jump PF kinetics were both assessed via inverse dynamics. Sprint speed, CMJ height and DJ reactive strength index defined task performances. Specific sprint and jump PF kinetics showed moderate-large correlations to task performances in 7 out of 9 relationships with peak positive power explaining 19-50% of the variance in the performance of these tasks (r/ρ = 0.434-0.706; p ≤ 0.024). Isometric PF strength, however, was unrelated to performance (CMJ: r = 0.126, DJ: r = 0.301, Sprint: ρ = 0.142), or task-specific PF kinetics during sprinting and jumping (all r ≤ 0.329). Dynamic task-specific function of the PF was an important component of overall performance, but this was not the case for isometric PF strength. These results highlight the distinctiveness of dynamic stretch-shortening cycle specific PF function compared to standing isometric PF strength for athletic performance.

title: Traumatic Proximal Rectus Femoris Avulsion With Recurrent Intramuscular Hematoma in a Competitive Martial Arts Athlete: A Case Report.
abstract: Proximal avulsion of the rectus femoris tendon is an uncommon injury in athletes and is rarely associated with direct trauma and extensive hematoma. We describe a 25-year-old competitive taekwondo athlete who developed acute hip flexor weakness and thigh swelling after a direct anterior thigh kick. Bedside musculoskeletal ultrasound demonstrated disruption of rectus femoris architecture with intramuscular hematoma, and magnetic resonance imaging confirmed complete avulsion of both proximal heads of the rectus femoris with tendon retraction and a large associated hematoma. The patient had sustained a recent prior quadriceps injury with hematoma. Recurrent hematoma development warranted hematologic testing, which revealed an isolated Factor VIII deficiency. Given his high functional demands, he underwent open surgical repair. This case highlights the importance of early imaging and consideration of operative management in high-level athletes presenting with trauma-related rectus femoris avulsion. It also highlights the importance of hematologic workups in athletes presenting with unexplained recurrent hematomas to effectively risk-stratify surgery and return to sport.

title: Creative Solution for Recurrent Failure of Flexor Tendon Repair.
abstract: Flexor tendon injuries present complex surgical and rehabilitative challenges, particularly in zone 2 of the hand. This article presents a case of recurrent flexor tendon failure in a young manual laborer, detailing initial repair, rupture, and secondary reconstruction. Despite multiple complications, including recurrent ruptures and repair failures, the case underscores the importance of individualized surgical planning, coordinated rehabilitation, and shared decision-making in achieving optimal functional recovery.

title: Examining the Impact of Supramaximal Eccentric and Long-Lever Isometric Training Protocols on Isometric Hamstring Strength, Nordic Hamstring Performance, and Sprint Speed.
abstract: The aim of this study was to compare the effects of a 6-week higher-volume eccentric training protocol with a combined lower-volume eccentric and long-lever isometric protocol on posterior chain strength and sprint performance. Thirty-three NCAA Division II soccer players (men: n = 17, age = 19.7 ± 1.2 years, height = 178.9 ± 6.6 cm, body mass 79.8 ± 8.1 kg; women: n = 16, age = 20.1 ± 0.9 years, height = 166.7 ± 5.2 cm, body mass = 67.0 ± 12.1 kg) were allocated to either group via exhaustive minimization. Nordic hamstring exercise break-point angle (NBPA), rapid isometric hamstring strength (LLB), 20m sprint performance, and continuous angular knee extension velocity waveforms were assessed pre- and post-intervention, and following a 2-week detraining period. A significant main effect of time was observed for sprint, NBPA, and rapid isometric strength (p < 0.05); however, Bonferroni-corrected within-group comparisons reached significance only for sprint performance in both groups, with no significant between-group differences for any outcome. Equivalence testing supported comparable sprint adaptations between protocols but could not be established for eccentric or isometric hamstring strength. All discrete outcome measures were largely maintained or continued to develop following the detraining period though range-specific eccentric strength appeared more sensitive to the training cessation. A combined low-volume eccentric and isometric training approach may represent a viable alternative to higher-volume eccentric programming for hamstring strength and speed development, although this should be approached cautiously to preserve neuromuscular qualities relevant to hamstring injury risk mitigation.

title: Association Between Hormone Variability and Anaerobic Performance in Recreationally Active Women: An Exploratory Study Using Mixed-Effect Location Scale Models.
abstract: Ramey, KT, Unrein, CL, Yang, C-H, and Hirsch, KR. Association between hormone variability and anaerobic performance in recreationally active women: An exploratory study using mixed-effect location scale models. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study explored the application of mixed-effects location scale modeling (MELS) to examine how daily variability in urinary estrogen (E), progesterone (PdG), and their ratio (E:P) relates to repeated sprint performance (peak power [PP], average power [AP], power drop [PD], and fatigue index [FI]) across low and high hormone phases in healthy, recreationally active eumenorrheic (n = 8) women and hormonal contraceptive users (intrauterine device = 6; oral contraception = 10; age: 24.7 ± 4.2 years; height: 165.5 ± 6.5 cm; body mass: 63.0 ± 6.7 kg). Subjects completed 30.4 ± 10.7 days of at-home urine hormone testing for E (ng⋅ml-1), PdG (µg⋅ml-1), and calculate E:P ratio. A repeated sprint test (10 × [6 seconds sprint: 30 seconds rest]) on a cycle ergometer was completed during both the low and high hormone phases to evaluate sprint performance. Fatigue index (%) was recorded, and PP (W), AP (W), and PD (W) were averaged across sprints. Associations between E, P, and E:P with FI, PP, AP, and PD were examined using separate MELS models. Paired t-tests assessed phase differences, and Pearson correlations evaluated relationships between day-of-testing hormone levels and performance. Day-of-testing E (p < 0.001), PdG (p < 0.001), PP (p = 0.047), and AP (p = 0.016) were significantly higher in the high hormone phase, and PdG correlated positively with PD (r = 0.574, p = 0.003). Greater individual E variability was associated with lower PP (Low: Estimate = -48.47, p = 0.004; High: Estimate = -50.18, p = 0.009) and AP (Low: Estimate = -46.75, p = 0.005; High: Estimate = -42.04, p = 0.024), remaining significant after controlling for percent body fat and lean mass (p = 0.008-0.022). These findings suggest hormonal instability may meaningfully influence anaerobic performance. This study introduces novel methodology and statistical framework that captures dynamic hormonal changes across the menstrual cycle and can be used to evaluate hormonal influence on female physiology and performance variability.

title: Jiawei Duhuo Jisheng Mixture Attenuates H2O2-induced Oxidative Injury and Osteogenic Dysfunction in Primary Osteoblasts: An Integrated Target Analysis and Experimental Validation.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Oxidative stress-induced osteoblast dysfunction is an important event in osteoporosis (OP). Jiawei Duhuo Jisheng Mixture (JDJM) is clinically used for bone-related disorders, but its molecular basis in OP remains unclear. This study explored OP-related candidate targets of JDJM and evaluated its cytoprotective effects in a hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)-induced primary osteoblast injury model.
METHODS: Candidate JDJM targets were predicted from its identified constituents and intersected with OP-related genes. The study integrated network-based and enrichment analyses with single-cell mapping, followed by molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulation. An H2O2-induced primary osteoblast injury model was used for experimental validation.
RESULTS: A total of 210 shared targets were identified. Network pharmacology and enrichment analyses implicated JDJM in the regulation of oxidative stress, inflammatory responses, extracellular matrix remodelling, osteogenesis and apoptosis, primarily through the MAPK, JAK-STAT and PI3K-Akt signalling pathways. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis further localized these candidate targets to osteogenic, stromal, vascular, and inflammatory cell populations. Molecular docking and dynamics simulations predicted stable interactions between representative JDJM-derived compounds and selected protein targets. In H2O2-injured primary osteoblasts, JDJM significantly reduced mean DCF fluorescence intensity, increased the alkaline phosphatase (ALP)-positive area and Alizarin Red S absorbance, and partially restored osteocalcin/bone Gla protein (OCN/BGP) protein and Bglap mRNA expression.JDJM was also associated with decreased total JAK1, STAT3, MAPK3, MMP9, and Bad expression and partial restoration of ESR1 expression.
DISCUSSION: JDJM attenuated H2O2-induced oxidative injury and osteogenic dysfunction in primary osteoblasts, accompanied by changes in JAK1, STAT3, MAPK3, MMP9, ESR1, and Bad expression. These results support a multi-target cytoprotective effect of JDJM under oxidative-stress conditions, although direct regulation of the corresponding signaling pathways remains to be confirmed.
CONCLUSION: JDJM attenuated H2O2-induced oxidative injury and partially restored osteogenic function in primary osteoblasts, accompanied by coordinated expression changes in JAK1, STAT3, MAPK3, MMP9, ESR1, and Bad. These findings support a multi-target protective effect of JDJM against oxidative stress-related osteoblast dysfunction.

title: The Influence of Menstrual Cycle Phase and Cramp Severity on Psychological Responses and Exercise Capacity in Physically Active Eumenorrheic Women.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The scientific literature is characterized by a historical underrepresentation of the female population in sports science. A critical issue in the current literature is the inconsistency between objectively measured (e.g., time to exhaustion) and subjectively perceived performance across the menstrual cycle. This inconsistency is often attributed to methodological limitations (e.g., absence of hormonal assessments and ovulation kits) and to the lack of consideration of menstrual-related symptoms and psychological variables.
PURPOSE: The primary objective of the study was to compare graded exercise test (GXT) performance outcomes across menstrual cycle phases. A secondary objective was to investigate whether cramp severity was associated with GXT performance during menses. A final objective was to examine the effects of menstrual cycle phase on psychological responses to exercise.
METHODS: Nineteen physically active eumenorrheic women (age 24 ± 4 years, V̇O2peak 38.4 ± 3.1 mL·kg -1·min -1) completed five GXTs: two for familiarization and three performed during experimental sessions scheduled in three specific phases of the menstrual cycle (menses, follicular, and luteal). Variables of interest included estradiol and progesterone levels, affective valence, arousal, anxiety, heart rate, rating of perceived exertion, mood disturbance, and motivation. Exercise capacity was operationalized as GXT performance outcomes (peak power output [Wpeak] and time to exhaustion). Cramp severity was measured only during menses.
RESULTS: No statistically significant differences in Wpeak or time to exhaustion were detected across menstrual cycle phases (p > 0.05). Secondary and exploratory regression analyses indicated that each one-point increase in menstrual cramp severity during menses was associated with lower GXT performance (Wpeak: -1.50 W; time to exhaustion: 2.72 s; p = 0.04; R 2 = ~0.35). Higher affective valence scores were associated with improved Wpeak (+4.27 W) and time to exhaustion (-8.51 s; p = 0.02; R 2 = ~0.36), whereas higher arousal scores were associated with lower Wpeak (-11.40 W) and higher time to exhaustion (6.47 s; p = 0.01; R 2 = ~0.46) across the menstrual cycle. Motivation was lower during menses than during the follicular phase (p = 0.04).
CONCLUSIONS: No statistically significant differences in GXT performance were detected across menstrual cycle phases. However, secondary and exploratory analyses suggest that greater menstrual cramp severity during menses was associated with lower time to exhaustion and Wpeak. These findings provide preliminary evidence that menstrual-related symptoms and psychological factors may contribute to variability in GXT performance outcomes and warrant further investigation in larger cohorts.
journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

title: Using High-Field Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy to Measure Muscle Glycogen in Patients With McArdle Disease.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION/AIMS: Patients with McArdle disease demonstrate exercise intolerance with muscle contractures and episodic rhabdomyolysis. Additionally, some patients show progressive fat replacement of paraspinal and shoulder muscles with aging. The cause of fat replacement in older McArdle patients is unknown but could relate to a higher glycogen accumulation in these muscles in line with what is found in Pompe disease. The aim of the study was to investigate if this is also the case in McArdle disease, which could imply that excess levels of glycogen accumulation are a potential driver of fat replacement of muscle.
METHODS: Using 7 Tesla 13C magnetic resonance spectroscopy, we measured glycogen noninvasively in lumbar, thigh, and calf muscles in 14 patients with McArdle disease and 19 healthy controls.
RESULTS: Patients with McArdle disease showed increased levels of glycogen in all muscles compared to controls; calf (3.2 times normal, p < 0.005), hamstrings (2.7 times normal, p < 0.005), anterior thigh compartment (2.7 times normal, p < 0.005), and lumbar muscle (2.1 times normal, p < 0.005). Glycogen was evenly distributed among muscle groups in both patients with McArdle disease and healthy controls.
DISCUSSION: Our results are in line with previous studies showing two to three times increased glycogen compared to control in muscle biopsies. We found no variability in glycogen concentration among muscles that could indicate glycogen as a predictor of muscle injury in McArdle disease.

title: Anti-inflammatory and Early Osteogenic Potential of a 96% Ethanol Extract of Drynaria bonii.
abstract:
ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Drynaria bonii H. Christ rhizome is traditionally used in Vietnamese medicine for fractures and musculoskeletal disorders. However, the effects of extraction solvent on chemical composition and biological activities relevant to the inflammatory and early mineralization phases of bone repair remain insufficiently defined.
AIM OF THE STUDY: This study compared 30%, 70%, and 96% ethanol extracts of D. bonii (DB30, DB70, and DB96, respectively) to identify a lead extract for further fracture-healing-oriented investigation.
METHODS: Rhizome extracts prepared with 30%, 70%, and 96% ethanol were profiled by ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography coupled with quadrupole time-of-flight tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC-QTOF-MS/MS). TNF-α inhibition was evaluated in LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages; acute anti-inflammatory activity was assessed in carrageenan-induced mouse paw edema; and calcium-associated staining was evaluated in canine mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) cultures using Alizarin Red S (ARS). Acute oral toxicity was assessed at 5000 mg/kg, and selected constituents were isolated from DB96. The four NMR-characterized constituents were subsequently evaluated by molecular docking against IκB kinase β (IKKβ).
RESULTS: The extracts showed distinct qualitative LC-MS/MS profiles, with DB70 displaying a broader curated phenolic/flavonoid profile and DB96 showing a different compositional pattern. DB96 produced the strongest TNF-α inhibition (IC50 = 32.05 μg/mL), compared with DB70 (63.73 μg/mL), whereas DB30 did not reach 50% inhibition at 100 μg/mL. DB96 also showed the largest numerical paw-edema inhibition among the extract groups at 1 and 24 h; however, statistical comparisons were performed only against the disease-control group and not among active treatment groups. In canine MSC cultures, DB96 at 50 μg/mL showed the highest descriptive normalized ARS-positive area among the extracts (12.0 ± 2.1%), although staining remained weak relative to the positive control and did not establish complete osteogenic differentiation. Betulin, ursolic acid, rutin, and kaempferol were isolated from DB96 and independently identified by NMR from a preparative DB96 batch. Among these constituents, ursolic acid and betulin showed the most favorable predicted IKKβ docking profiles, with binding energies of -8.52 and -8.41 kcal/mol, respectively. No mortality or overt acute toxicity was observed for any of the three extracts after a single oral dose of 5000 mg/kg.
CONCLUSION: The findings support DB96 as the lead extract among the three preparations for subsequent mechanistic and bone-repair-oriented investigation. Docking provided complementary mechanistic support for possible interactions of selected DB96 constituents with IKKβ, but did not establish direct target inhibition. Direct fracture-healing efficacy, definitive osteogenic differentiation, quantitative constituent enrichment, and repeated-dose safety remain to be established.

title: Reduction in Force Complexity Following Eccentric Exercise That Elicits Exercise-Induced Muscle Damage.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Unaccustomed eccentric exercise has been shown to lead to muscle damage. Previous research suggests that fatigue reduces the complexity of muscle force output. However, previous research has not investigated whether the force complexity response to fatigue is affected by eccentric exercise. Therefore, the purpose of the present study was to examine the effect of eccentric exercise and a subsequent fatiguing task on force variability and complexity.
METHODS: Twelve individuals (six females) participated in the study. The participants performed eccentric exercise consisting of six sets of 10 repetitions of the knee extensors to elicit muscle damage. Before and 48 hr after eccentric exercise, the participants were assessed for maximal voluntary contraction and performed a sustained isometric time to task failure protocol at 25% of maximal voluntary contraction. Force variability was assessed in the first 10 s (Fresh) and last 10 s (End-Task) of the time to task failure via standard deviation, coefficient of variation, detrended fluctuation analysis, sample entropy, and multiscale sample entropy.
RESULTS: Maximal voluntary contraction (532.67 ± 177.49 N vs. 448.54 ± 186.92 N, p < .001) and time to task failure (197.10 ± 44.81 s vs. 157.70 ± 62.52 s, p = .031) were reduced after eccentric exercise. There were no differences in force variability following eccentric exercise at either the Fresh or End-Task time points. Force complexity was reduced at both Fresh (detrended fluctuation analysis: 1.37 ± 0.18 vs. 1.47 ± 0.21; sample entropy: 0.88 ± 0.27 vs. 0.71 ± 0.027) and End-Task (sample entropy: 0.63 ± 0.17 vs. 0.53 ± 0.15), following eccentric exercise compared with the pre-eccentric exercise condition.
CONCLUSIONS: Reductions in force complexity, but not force variability, were observed following eccentric exercise. These changes are thought to be due to changes in motor control strategies to compensate for damaged tissue.

title: Propionibacterium cheese and bone turnover in active young adults: a randomized-controlled trial.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Young physically active individuals exposed to prolonged physiological stress and low energy availability are prone to reduced gonadal steroid protection and increased bone turnover. Nutritional strategies that favor positive bone remodeling balance are of clinical interest. Jarlsberg cheese contains Propionibacterium freudenreichii (PF), which produces vitamin K₂ and 1,4-dihydroxy-2-naphthoic acid (DHNA), compounds with potential favorable effects on bone health.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this 24-week sex-stratified randomized-controlled trial, 60 young physically active adults engaged in endurance training were allocated to daily intake of either Jarlsberg cheese or a nutritionally comparable control cheese without PF. The primary outcome was change in serum total osteocalcin (tOC). Secondary outcomes were changes in carboxylated osteocalcin (cOC), procollagen type 1 N-terminal propeptide (P1NP), cross-linked C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (CTX), P1NP/CTX ratio, lumbar spine bone mineral density (BMD), and trabecular bone score (TBS).
RESULTS: After 24 weeks, serum tOC was significantly higher in the Jarlsberg group than in controls (38.0 vs. 26.8 ng/mL, p < 0.01). cOC and P1NP/CTX ratio increased in favor of the Jarlsberg group (p = 0.03). Lumbar spine BMD increased in the Jarlsberg group (mean change 0.012 g/cm2, p = 0.03), with a greater increase than in controls (p = 0.05), and TBS showed a positive trend in the Jarlsberg group.
CONCLUSION: Daily intake of cheese-containing PF was associated with favorable changes in bone turnover markers and increase in lumbar spine BMD. These findings suggest that PF-fermented cheese may support bone metabolism in young individuals exposed to reduced hormonal protection and high bone turnover.
PROTOCOL NUMBER: XCS-Jarlsberg/IIA.
CLINICALTRIALS: GOV: NCT06688032.
journal: Journal of bone and mineral metabolism

title: Radial pressure wave treatment accelerates recovery from immobilization-induced soleus muscle atrophy and improves ankle range of motion in mice.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Disuse muscle atrophy following immobilization is characterized by decreased muscle mass and reduced joint range of motion (ROM). Radial pressure wave (RPW) treatment is a non-invasive modality that delivers mechanical energy to musculoskeletal tissues, but its efficacy in skeletal muscle recovery from disuse atrophy remains largely unknown. We examined whether RPW treatment accelerates soleus muscle structural recovery and passive ankle dorsiflexion ROM following immobilization-induced atrophy in mice. Furthermore, we investigated the underlying molecular signaling cascades and gene expression profiles associated with RPW-mediated recovery.

Soleus muscle mass, fiber cross-sectional area (CSA), and passive ankle dorsiflexion ROM were assessed. Candidate genes identified as differentially expressed by exploratory RNA-sequencing in one mouse per group ([Formula: see text]) were subsequently evaluated by quantitative PCR and immunoblotting across all animals in the full cohort ([Formula: see text] per group).
RESULTS: RPW treatment increased fiber CSA to [Formula: see text] (vs. [Formula: see text] in the sham group) and improved ankle dorsiflexion ROM to [Formula: see text] (vs. [Formula: see text]). Gene set enrichment analysis revealed suppression of the forkhead box O (FoxO) signaling pathway and enrichment of the extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling pathway. Igf1 expression was higher in the RPW group ([Formula: see text]-fold vs. sham: [Formula: see text]-fold), accompanied by elevated Akt phosphorylation. title: Beyond a mechanical cushion: the paracrine secretome of the infrapatellar fat pad in knee homeostasis and osteoarthritis.
abstract: The Infrapatellar Fat Pad (IFP), traditionally regarded as a passive adipose structure providing mechanical support within the knee, is increasingly recognized as an immunometabolic organ that shapes the intra-articular microenvironment through its paracrine secretome. Understanding these interactions may clarify Osteoarthritis (OA) pathophysiology and inform new diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. This narrative review examined current evidence on the paracrine role of the IFP in knee OA. We focused on its anatomy and cellular composition; cytokines, adipokines, growth factors, matrix-remodeling mediators, and extracellular vesicles; and interactions with cartilage, synovium, subchondral bone, and resident immune cells. Current evidence indicates that the IFP regulates the joint microenvironment through a network of paracrine mediators. Under physiological conditions, its secretome supports tissue homeostasis, repair, and immune regulation. In OA, secretome dysregulation promotes chronic inflammation, extracellular matrix degradation, fibrosis, angiogenesis, and pain sensitization. Emerging findings also suggest that the IFP may provide biomarkers and therapeutic targets for regenerative and disease-modifying strategies. The IFP should be regarded as a biologically active immunometabolic organ involved in knee OA initiation and progression. Better characterization of its secretome may refine OA phenotyping, support biomarker discovery and patient stratification, and guide precision-medicine and disease-modifying approaches.

title: Estrogen and Lysyl Oxidase: How Crosslink Changes Increase Biological Female Athlete ACL Injury Risk.
abstract: Across sports that involve cutting, pivoting, and single-leg jump landings, biological female athletes sustain anterior cruciate ligament injuries at 2- to 9-fold greater rates than males. The mechanical resilience of the anterior cruciate ligament depends on extracellular matrix stabilization. Crosslinking, primarily mediated by lysyl oxidase, is essential to extracellular matrix maturation, to resisting the tensile and shear forces encountered during athletic activity, and to long-term anterior cruciate ligament health. Estrogen-mediated lysyl oxidase modulation may weaken the extracellular matrix, reducing its capacity to withstand mechanical loads. This narrative review explores how estrogen influences lysyl oxidase function, particularly in the context of collagen crosslinking and connective tissue health. Special emphasis is placed on biological female anterior cruciate ligament injury risk, a highly relevant example of clinical estrogen-associated extracellular matrix vulnerability. By integrating epidemiologic evidence with emerging molecular and mechanistic data, clinicians are provided with a contemporary biologically informed perspective on sex-specific anterior cruciate ligament injury risk. Future research and prevention strategies are discussed.

title: Optimising Pre-race Physical Preparation for Sprint Events at Major Championships Under New Rule Changes and Competition Formats.
abstract: Championship sprint outcomes are often decided by margins as small as hundredths or even thousandths of a second, placing great importance on optimising every aspect of race-day preparation. At major championships, the interval between warm-up and race start includes time in a designated Call Room and can exceed 50 min, long enough to compromise the physiological benefits of the warm-up. Whilst this delay is not new, recent World Athletics technology regulations prohibit heated garments in the Call Room, and athletes must now enter the track wearing only their race kit, making muscle temperature and neuromuscular readiness harder to maintain. The addition of mixed relay events further increases exposure to repeated pre-race transition periods. This leading article therefore reviews the determinants of sprint performance most sensitive to the pre-race period and evaluates acute strategies that may help preserve or restore readiness on the day of competition. Particular attention is given to evidence-informed strategies that complement the main warm-up and can be implemented within current competition regulations. Passive heat maintenance and plyometric conditioning activities appear to offer the greatest practical relevance within current Call Room constraints, with maintenance of muscle temperature an important consideration for preserving sprint and power performance. While there is relevant supporting research, no study has simulated the exact demands of a major championship sprint event, and recommendations therefore rest on mechanistic rationale and applied practice as well as direct evidence. These include a same-day priming session ~ 4-6 h before competition, passive insulation to attenuate muscle temperature decline during the transition period, and a brief plyometric or short acceleration stimulus 8-16 min before race start, with athletes encouraged to establish their individual responses in training and simulated competition.

title: Intensity-dependent microcurrent stimulation enhances BMSC-derived cartilage microtissue formation under defined culture conditions.
abstract: Engineering phenotypically favorable cartilage-like tissue from bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) remains challenging because chondrogenic differentiation can be accompanied by insufficient cartilage-associated extracellular matrix accumulation and unfavorable hypertrophic and catabolic responses. Here, we established a microcurrent-assisted culture system for scaffold-free BMSC-derived cartilage microtissues (CMTs) and investigated the intensity-dependent effects of continuous unidirectional direct-current stimulation at 0, 50, 100, 150, 250, or 500 μA under a defined electrical and culture configuration. Among the tested conditions, 150 μA (nominal electrode current density, 3 μA/mm2) showed the most consistently favorable overall response, with enhanced cartilage-associated gene and protein expression, greater type II collagen- and glycosaminoglycan-rich matrix accumulation, improved CMT morphology, and higher apparent mechanical properties. In contrast, 250 and 500 μA were associated with reduced cartilage-associated matrix formation and increased fibrotic, hypertrophic, catabolic, inflammatory, and apoptosis-related markers. The 150 μA condition was also associated with a distinct intracellular Ca2+ response pattern and increased NFATc1 nuclear localization; verapamil, BAPTA-AM, and cyclosporin A attenuated NFATc1 nuclear localization, supporting involvement of Ca2+/calcineurin/NFAT-related signaling without establishing a unique causal mechanism. After 2 weeks of xenogeneic subcutaneous implantation in nude mice, CMTs preconditioned at 150 μA exhibited greater cartilage-like matrix accumulation and higher apparent compressive properties than those preconditioned at 0 or 500 μA. These findings identify 150 μA as the best-performing tested condition under the present electrical configuration and provide short-term ectopic proof-of-concept evidence, while longer-term orthotopic studies are required to evaluate phenotypic stability, tissue integration, and functional outcomes in cartilage-defect models.

title: Strain-Stabilization of Collagen in Heart Valve Tissues: A Biomechanical Account of Proteolysis.
abstract: A heart valve leaflet flexes tens of millions of times each year inside a fluid carrying active collagenases, yet its collagen network holds for decades before disease unravels it within months. This review argues the resolving principle is mechanical. Tensile strain reshapes the collagen triple helix and folds its scissile bond away from matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), a protective behavior termed strain-stabilization. The mechanism is traced from reconstituted collagen and tendon to native semilunar valve leaflets under physiologically realistic biaxial loading. The organizing framework is a V-shaped force-degradation curve-a schematic, cross-scale synthesis assembled from experiments that differ in enzyme type, length scale, and tissue system, rather than a single directly measured dose-response relationship. Enzymatic attack is rapid at zero strain, falls to a minimum under moderate physiological tension, and rises under pathological overload, where single-molecule measurements record a 100-fold increase in MMP-1 cleavage rate at ∼10 pN. Two biaxial studies anchor the argument. Equibiaxial stretching of porcine leaflets accelerated collagenolysis, whereas loading matched to diastolic strain ratios suppressed it almost entirely. Crimp, fiber rotation, and heterogeneous recruitment govern how tissue-level strain reaches individual molecules and which arm of the V-curve a leaflet occupies. Glutaraldehyde-fixed bioprosthetic valves fail by this logic inverted: fixation freezes the helix, disables the protective cycle, and strips glycosaminoglycans from the interfibrillary space before implantation. Conditioning tissue-engineered scaffolds under physiological biaxial strain produces collagen anisotropy matching native leaflets and tunes valve interstitial cell biosynthesis toward a homeostatic phenotype. Loading is a design variable, and the converging evidence reviewed here suggests that a valve can in principle be engineered to maintain its collagen in the protected regime-a hypothesis that tissue-engineering studies are now beginning to test experimentally.

title: A distributed event-triggered framework for coordinating athlete autonomic states via wearable sensor networks.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Interpersonal autonomic physiology (IAP) research has established that physiological synchrony (PS), the temporal interdependence of autonomic nervous system (ANS) activity across individuals, is an established phenomenon in team-based settings. However, PS in athlete cohorts has been studied exclusively as a passive observational variable; no framework actively regulates autonomic coherence under the communication constraints of wireless body area networks. This study integrates IAP and distributed control theory by formulating team-level autonomic coherence as a leaderless multi-agent consensus problem.
METHODS: Each wearable unit was modeled as a two-dimensional linear agent whose state encodes cardiovascular autonomic tone (parasympathetic index: HRV-RMSSD) and sympathetic arousal load (EDA skin-conductance level, SCL), consistent with the Banister Fitness-Fatigue Model. Initial model states were derived from ECG/EDA records of WESAD subjects S2-S7, used only to provide heterogeneous simulation initial conditions (correlations were directional, non-significant sanity checks: r = -0.71, p = 0.114 for RMSSD; r = 0.68, p = 0.137 for SCL; N = 6). Three engineering challenges were addressed: (i) BLE communication delays h c ∈ [15, 150] ms; (ii) neuromuscular input delays h i ∈ [150, 300] ms; and (iii) switching directed topologies from dynamic team formations. A distributed dynamic event-triggered mechanism (DETM) drove all agents toward consensus while transmitting data only upon detection of meaningful state deviation. Stability was established via a dual-integral Lyapunov-Krasovskii functional, with LMI feasibility verified by CVXPY (ε = 0.087). Simulations ran for 300 s under three delay scenarios with five initial-condition perturbation folds; battery life was estimated from a four-component nRF52840 energy model.
RESULTS: The proposed DETM reduced BLE transmissions by 38.38% in the nominal case while achieving convergence of the normalized model states within 4-7 s. A Zeno-free guarantee (T min = 0.06 s) and a theoretical battery-life estimate of about 36 days were obtained. The ablation analysis attributed the largest communication saving to the dynamic internal variable ρ i (t) and the largest convergence-time improvement to the dual-delay structure. Five initial-condition perturbation folds indicated numerical robustness to the starting states.
DISCUSSION: These findings support control-theoretic and network-level feasibility only. Athlete studies are required before physiological benefits, safety, or real-world effectiveness can be inferred.

title: Diffuse Bilateral Multifocal Bone Stress Injuries in a 19-Year-Old Male Military Trainee: A Case Report.
abstract: Bone stress injuries (BSIs) are common among high-performance athletes and military trainees. BSIs typically present with point tenderness, loading pain, and nighttime discomfort, and most involve only one or two bones, with clinical symptoms roughly proportional to the degree of osseous injury. We present the case of a 19-year-old male engaged in high-intensity Air Force Special Warfare training who initially presented with vague low back, thigh, and foot pain and was ultimately diagnosed with diffuse multifocal grade 3 and 4a BSIs involving numerous bones of the bilateral lower extremities. What makes this case unusual is the extent and severity of osseous injury relative to the patient's comparatively mild and nonspecific symptoms. Further, the case demonstrates the complexity of bone stress pathology and highlights the possibility that reduced physical activity during adolescence contributed to later bone fragility.

title: Foot-strike angle affects performance and injury risk during cutting in soccer athletes.
abstract: Female soccer athletes experience elevated rates of non-contact anterior cruciate ligament injuries, particularly during cutting tasks that require rapid energy absorption and generation at the knee. This study examined the effects of sex and fatigue on knee joint power and foot‑strike angle during unanticipated cutting in cleated footwear. Twenty athletes (10 M/10F) completed unanticipated cuts before and after a standardized fatigue protocol. Kinematic and kinetic data were collected, and knee joint power and foot‑strike angle were calculated using standard inverse dynamics. Neither sex nor fatigue significantly influenced peak positive knee joint power (p > 0.05), although greater power was associated with faster approach velocities (p = 0.040). In contrast, peak negative knee joint power was greater in females, indicating a greater rate of energy absorption at the knee (p = 0.027). Foot‑strike angle differed by sex (p = 0.026), with females demonstrating greater angles at initial contact. A moderate negative correlation was observed between foot‑strike angle and peak negative knee joint power (r = -0.64, p = 0.005). These findings suggest that sex-related differences in cutting strategy may influence how energy is absorbed at the knee, with foot‑strike emerging as a potential contributor to these mechanical patterns.

title: QT Interval Prolongation in Athletes With Negative Genetic Testing and Complete Normalization After Detraining.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: QT interval prolongation is traditionally associated with congenital or acquired long QT syndrome; however, its interpretation in athletes remains challenging because of possible exercise-induced electrophysiological adaptations.
CASE SUMMARY: We report a case series of 4 competitive athletes referred to our Sports Cardiology clinic after incidental detection of marked QT interval prolongation during preparticipation screening for sports eligibility. All individuals were asymptomatic, took no QT interval-prolonging drugs, had normal electrolyte levels, and had negative family screening and genetic testing. Following a detraining period of 3-6 months, repeat electrocardiograms showed consistent normalization of both QT interval and corrected QT intervals in all cases. The magnitude of the corrected QT interval reduction was substantial and observed intraindividually, independently of significant changes in heart rate.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings support the concept that, in some athletes, QT interval prolongation may represent a dynamic and reversible phenotype related to training load, termed "exercise-induced" long QT interval. Recognition of this pattern may help avoid misdiagnosis of congenital long QT syndrome and inappropriate restriction from competitive sports, although its long-term arrhythmic risk remains unclear.

title: A rare traumatic triad: Open bicondylar non-conjoint Hoffa fracture with partial tibial tubercle and medial epicondyle avulsions - A case report and biomechanical analysis.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Coronal shear fractures of the distal femoral condyles are rare intra-articular injuries, and the simultaneous occurrence of a non-conjoint bicondylar Hoffa fracture with a partial anterior tibial tubercle avulsion and a medial epicondyle avulsion constitutes an exceptionally complex traumatic triad. We report the case of a 35-year-old male motorcyclist who sustained this "floating" articular block injury (AO/OTA 33-B3.3) following a high-velocity accident. Diagnostic assessment utilizing Computed Tomography with 3D reconstruction revealed a vertical Letenneur Type II fracture of the medial condyle and a comminuted Letenneur Type I fracture of the lateral condyle, complicated by significant rotational instability. Surgical management prioritized the posterior femoral instability through a double posterior approach, which allowed for direct visualization and anatomical reduction. Fixation was achieved using posterior-to-anterior headless compression screws, augmented by a posterior buttress plate on the lateral column to neutralize shear forces, while the medial epicondyle was anatomically reduced and fixed; the stable partial tibial tubercle avulsion was treated conservatively. At the two-year follow-up, the patient demonstrated excellent functional recovery with 120 degrees of flexion, a Lysholm score of 91, and a successful return to recreational sports. This case highlights the importance of the double posterior approach and "targeted rigidity" in managing multidirectional instability, permitting early mobilization even in the presence of complex extensor mechanism involvement.
INTRODUCTION: Coronal shear fractures of the distal femoral condyles (Hoffa fractures) are rare intra-articular injuries, with bicondylar patterns being exceptionally uncommon. A non-conjoint bicondylar Hoffa fracture combined with a partial anterior tibial tubercle (ATT) avulsion and a medial epicondyle avulsion represents a complex, "floating" articular block that challenges standard treatment algorithms. This case report analyzes the biomechanics and management of this rare traumatic triad.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 35-year-old male motorcyclist presented with a Gustilo-Anderson Type I open knee injury following a high-velocity crash involving hyper-flexion and valgus stress. CT imaging confirmed a non-conjoint bicondylar Hoffa fracture (AO/OTA 33-B3.3, Bagaria Type 3). The lateral condyle presented as a Letenneur Type I fracture with extensive comminution, while the medial condyle was a Letenneur Type II vertical fracture. Associated injuries included an Ogden Type I partial ATT avulsion and a Watson-Jones Type I medial epicondyle avulsion.Surgical management utilized a double posterior approach to visualize and reduce the posterior fragments. Fixation involved headless cannulated compression screws for both condyles, augmented by a posterior buttress plate on the lateral column to resist shear forces. The medial epicondyle was refixed with a screw and washer, while the stable ATT avulsion was managed conservatively. At the two-year follow-up, the patient achieved excellent functional outcomes, including 120° of flexion, a Lysholm score of 91, and a Tegner Activity Scale score of 7.
CONCLUSION: Managing this complex triad requires a thorough understanding of the injury mechanism, which involves coronal shear, valgus stress, and eccentric extensor loading. 3D CT reconstruction is mandatory for planning, and a double posterior approach provides superior visualization for anatomical reduction and posterior-to-anterior fixation. Rigid fixation, particularly using anti-glide plating for the lateral column, permits early mobilization and the conservative management of stable associated injuries, leading to high patient satisfaction.

title: Precision Diagnostics in Bone Disease: The Potential of Circulating and Stem Cell-Associated miRNAs as Minimally Invasive Biomarkers.
abstract: Stem cell-associated microRNAs (miRNAs) have emerged as pivotal regulators of osteogenesis, influencing lineage commitment, differentiation, and skeletal tissue homeostasis. Their dysregulation has been increasingly linked to a spectrum of osteogenic disorders, including osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, and impaired fracture healing. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on the diagnostic potential of stem cell-associated miRNAs in bone-related pathologies. We highlight their roles in modulating osteoblast and osteoclast activity, maintaining mesenchymal stem cell fate, and orchestrating signaling pathways such as Wnt/β-catenin, bone morphogenetic protein, and Notch. Particular emphasis is placed on circulating miRNAs as minimally invasive biomarkers, offering prospects for early detection, disease stratification, and monitoring therapeutic response. Furthermore, we discuss methodological advances in miRNA profiling, challenges in clinical translation, and the need for standardized validation frameworks. By integrating molecular insights with translational perspectives, this review underscores the promise of stem cell-associated miRNAs as diagnostic tools in osteogenic disorders, while identifying critical gaps that must be addressed to enable their incorporation into precision medicine strategies.

title: Muscle satellite cell dysfunction in critical illness: niche biology, regenerative failure, and implications for recovery.
abstract: Adult skeletal muscle can regenerate. After muscle injury, muscle stem cells (satellite cells) can generate new muscle fibers. Under normal conditions, satellite cells are mitotically quiescent and located beneath the basal lamina of muscle fibers. In response to regenerative stimuli, satellite cells activate and proliferate as myogenic precursor cells. After several rounds of cell division, these precursor cells differentiate and fuse to form new muscle fibers. A subset of proliferating myogenic precursor cells returns to a quiescent state to replenish the satellite cell pool through self-renewal. Intensive care unit-acquired weakness (ICU-AW) affects many critically ill patients partly due to acute muscle loss. It is a major physical component of post-intensive care syndrome. Current explanations of ICU-AW focus on rapid protein breakdown and impaired energy metabolism during the early catabolic phase, but these mechanisms do not fully explain why some survivors fail to rebuild muscle once the initial catabolic stress has subsided. In this review, we argue that persistent weakness may also reflect defective muscle regeneration, with satellite cell dysfunction and niche abnormalities as plausible contributors. Recent serial-biopsy studies suggest that dysfunction can occur without stem-cell depletion: satellite cell number can be preserved even when differentiation or later proliferative capacity is impaired in culture. We first review the normal satellite cell niche, including the parent fiber, microvasculature and perivascular cells, extracellular matrix, resident immune and interstitial cells, and systemic signals, with separate consideration of the diaphragm. We then examine how critical illness affects these compartments and how cell-intrinsic defects may additionally impair regeneration. We use this evidence to develop three working hypotheses (niche-detached activation, abortive myogenesis, and niche locking) and treat them as testable models rather than recognized mechanisms. Finally, we consider how future studies might measure, target, and test these processes.

title: Extreme energy expenditure during a 200 km three-day open-water swim: A doubly labeled water case study.
abstract: The upper limits of total energy expenditure (TEE) in humans have primarily been described during single-day ultra-endurance events, or during multistage land-based endurance events across several days. However, little is known about the physiological limits of sustained energy turnover during shorter multi-day, near-continuous exercise events, particularly when performed in an aquatic environment. Prolonged immersion in water imposes substantial thermoregulatory demands due to increased conductive heat loss, which may further elevate metabolic requirements beyond those observed in (cold) land-based events. The 200 km Elfstedentocht swim, completed over approximately three days with minimal sleep and near-continuous swimming, provides a unique opportunity to investigate the upper limits of human energy expenditure during prolonged multi-day exercise in water. In this case study, we therefore assessed TEE in a former Olympic athlete (mass 103 kg, height 2.04 m, age 38 years) during a 200-km swim completed over 3 days using doubly labeled water. TEE was 195 Megajoule (MJ) (46,700 kcals), corresponding to 6.17x basal metabolic rate over the three-day period. This TEE is among the highest TEE reported thus far over similar periods, suggesting that the combined near-continuous exercise and imposed sustained thermoregulatory demands due to conductive heat loss lead to extreme energy expenditure. Notably, the absolute energy expenditure of ∼14,700 kcal per day exceeds previous limits.

title: Therapeutic Limb Hypothermia Preserves Neurophysiologic Function and Reduces Tissue Injury in a Novel Porcine Survival Model of Acute Hindlimb Ischemia.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Acute limb ischemia carries high morbidity and risk of limb loss. Prior animal models were limited to non-survival designs and biochemical endpoints, precluding assessment of long-term outcomes. We developed a porcine survival model of ischemia-reperfusion injury to evaluate therapeutic limb hypothermia with functional, neurophysiologic, and histopathologic endpoints.
METHODS: Ten female Yorkshire pigs underwent unilateral hindlimb ischemia via balloon occlusion of the ipsilateral external and internal iliac arteries for six hours, confirmed by angiography, and were randomized to hypothermia (5°C) or normothermia, with the contralateral limb as control. Hypothermia was applied via a closed-loop limb-cooling device to achieve goal muscle temperature. Animals were monitored for 7 days with daily Tarlov assessment and underwent terminal neurophysiologic testing and muscle/nerve biopsy on day 7.
RESULTS: Hypothermia-treated limbs showed significantly preserved sensory and motor nerve conduction at POD7 versus marked loss in controls (p = 0.008 for both SNAP and CMAP preservation), and markedly reduced histologic muscle injury across degeneration, necrosis, inflammation, and regeneration (cumulative score, p < 0.001). Nerve histologic injury did not differ significantly between groups (p = 0.45), and gait recovery showed a favorable but non-significant trend versus controls (p = 0.34).
CONCLUSION: Localized limb hypothermia preserves neurophysiologic function and reduces tissue injury after acute limb ischemia (p ≤ 0.008 for both), with a favorable but non-significant trend in functional recovery. This novel large-animal model is relevant for studying human acute limb ischemia and reperfusion injury in traumatic or embolic settings.

title: Young Investigator Award: Where Do We Start? A Conceptual Model for Implementing Menstrual Cycle Tracking in Sport.
abstract: Menstrual cycle tracking is a much-discussed component of the ' female athlete' research theme; however, more translational work is needed to meet practitioners' desire for further guidance on the implementation of tracking in applied settings. The purpose of this paper is to present a preliminary conceptual model to inform practitioners' decision-making around menstrual cycle tracking and assist researchers in identifying and framing future research directions. The proposed model-Conducting and Navigating menstrual cycle Education, Communication and Tracking (ConNECT)-proposes that communication and education strategies may be utilised to affect social, organisational and individual level change, ultimately supporting the implementation of menstrual cycle tracking by increasing its uptake and impact. This model was developed based on the findings from a series of studies conducted by the authors, which considered the existing literature on tracking and the perspectives of athletes and practitioners. Therefore, the ConNECT model offers an ecologically sound starting point for sport scientists, coaches and other members of an athlete's support team to base their practice on.

title: Bioengineered skeletal muscle construct using a cell-seeded decellularized diaphragm muscle scaffolding system for pelvic muscle regeneration.
abstract: Pelvic floor muscle injury often leads to dysfunction of the entire pelvic urogenital system, negatively impacting the patient's quality of life. Current treatment options include autologous muscle transfer and biomaterial-based meshes and slings; however, adequately restoring muscle function remains a significant challenge. With advances in skeletal muscle tissue engineering, bioengineered skeletal muscle constructs have emerged as promising therapeutic solutions for treating various types of muscle injuries. Recently, these strategies have been expanded to address injuries involving pelvic musculature. In this study, we developed a bioengineered skeletal muscle construct by seeding human muscle progenitor cells (hMPCs) onto a decellularized skeletal muscle scaffold to regenerate damaged pelvic muscle tissues. Allogeneic decellularized diaphragm muscle tissue was employed as a biological scaffold due to its structural and mechanical similarities to native pelvic muscle tissues. We demonstrated that the decellularized diaphragm retained aligned skeletal muscle matrix microstructures and preserved mechanical properties. hMPCs seeded on the decellularized scaffold remained viable and differentiated into aligned muscle fibers. The feasibility of the bioengineered muscle construct was investigated in a rat model of extensive pelvic muscle injury. Our in vivo results demonstrated that the implanted construct supported the formation of new skeletal muscle tissue with vascular and neural integration and improved recovery of muscle weight and function. To our knowledge, this is the first approach using decellularized diaphragm muscle tissue matrices as a biologic scaffold for pelvic muscle repair. With further advances, this approach may offer an alternative strategy for repairing pelvic muscle injuries. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Pelvic floor muscle injury significantly impairs quality of life, yet current mesh- and sling-based treatments are limited by poor structural and biological integration. Here, we developed a bioengineered skeletal muscle construct using human muscle progenitor cells seeded onto a decellularized diaphragm scaffold, given its biomimetic architecture and mechanical properties that closely resemble native pelvic floor muscle. In a rat model of pelvic floor injury, this construct promoted muscle regeneration, vascularization, and neural integration while improving muscle mass and function. To our knowledge, this is the first use of decellularized diaphragm tissue for pelvic muscle reconstruction. This approach may provide a promising strategy for supporting structural and functional muscle repair.

title: Osteogenic priming of canine perivascular mesenchymal stromal cells enhances extracellular vesicle yield and in vitro activity for bone regeneration.
abstract: The therapeutic efficacy of mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) is intrinsically linked to their response to the host microenvironment by the interplay with resident cells. While MSC-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) offer a promising cell-free alternative, optimizing their production and cargo for specific clinical applications remains a challenge. We investigated the impact of in vitro osteogenic priming on the yield, molecular profile, and functional activity of EVs derived from canine umbilical cord perivascular MSCs (cPMSCs). The EVs secreted by osteogenic primed and naïve cPMSC were isolated by ultracentrifugation and characterized by nanoparticle tracking analysis, western blotting, and electronic transmission microscopy. In vitro functional assays of cellular uptake, proliferation, migration, and mineralization were performed. MicroRNAs known to participate in osteogenesis (cfa-miR-21, cfa-miR26a, cfa-miR-27a and cfa-miR-29a) were evaluated in EV samples of both groups through RT-qPCR. Notably, osteogenic priming led to a 1.5-fold increase in vesicle yield (5.6 ± 0.5 ×1010 particles/ml) compared to naïve MSCs (3.7 ± 0.7 ×1010 particles/ml), without altering vesicle distribution nor TSG101 expression (similar expression for both groups). Functional assays revealed that while both EV populations were efficiently internalized, osteogenic priming significantly improved extracellular matrix mineralization (P=0.0003) and enhanced EV-mediated cell migration (P=0.005). Molecular analysis confirmed the enrichment of key osteogenic microRNAs, including cfa-miR-21, cfa-miR-26a, cfa-miR-27a, and cfa-miR-29a, in both groups. These findings demonstrate that osteogenic priming is a robust strategy to improve EV production efficiency and migratory potential, providing a molecularly characterized foundation for advanced cell-free orthopedic therapies in veterinary medicine.

title: Aerobic Exercise Ameliorates Osteoarthritic Chondrocyte Degradation in Osteoarthritis via Regulating E2F8/NLRP14 Signaling Pathway.
abstract: Although physical activity is known to mitigate disease risks, its protective molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. E2F8, a regulator of cell cycle and metabolism, showed significant differential expression between osteoarthritis (OA) and exercise models, suggesting it may link mechanical activity to OA alleviation. In vitro, Interleukin-1 Beta (IL-1β) simulated inflammation. In vivo, OA was induced in rats via Monosodium iodoacetate (MIA) injection. The effects of E2F8 and mechanical stress were assessed using moderate treadmill exercise, histology, and joint observation. Bioinformatic analysis, cyclic tensile strain, Western blot, immunofluorescence, and gene knockdown were used to investigate mechanisms. In OA rats, E2F8 was downregulated in cartilage while NLRP14 increased. Exercise reversed E2F8 downregulation, alleviated cartilage degeneration, restored anabolic activity, and reduced inflammatory catabolism linked to senescence. In vitro, mechanical stress reversed the IL-1β-induced anabolic/catabolic imbalance by regulating the E2F8/NLRP14, mitigating OA progression. Mechanical stress enhances E2F8 expression in osteoarthritic chondrocytes, which in turn protects cartilage by suppressing the expression of NLRP14. These findings underscore the role of E2F8 as a mechano-sensitive mediator and highlight the potential of exercise or exercise-mimetic therapies as effective strategies for preventing and treating OA.

title: A multifunctional MOF-mineralized conductive hydrogel coating on zinc implants orchestrates neuro-osteogenic coupling for enhanced bone defect repair.
abstract: Zinc (Zn)-based implants face critical challenges in clinical orthopedic applications due to rapid corrosion, localized Zn2+-induced cytotoxicity, and inadequate osteogenic activity. Herein, we report a metal-organic framework (MOF)-mediated mineralization strategy to engineer a multifunctional conductive hydrogel coating on pure zinc substrates, integrated with polypyrrole nanoparticles (Ppy NPs). This hierarchical coating design significantly enhances interfacial adhesion and reduces the in vitro corrosion volume ratio of zinc substrates by approximately 53.23% after 14 days of immersion, effectively mitigating excessive degradation-associated ion release. The MOF- mediated mineralized layer provides controlled Zn2+/Cu2+ release and stabilizes the implant interface, while Ppy NPs establish an intrinsic electroactive microenvironment. These synergistic ionic and electrical cues promote Schwann cell functional activity, enhance neurotrophic factor secretion, and subsequently facilitate mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) osteogenic differentiation through neuro-osteogenic communication. Notably, co-culture of MSCs with Schwann cells on the Zn/H@MP coating surface results in a 257% increase in alkaline phosphatase activity and a 222% enhancement in mineralized nodule formation compared to MSC mono-culture, accompanied by significant upregulation of key osteogenic markers, demonstrating the neuro-osteogenic coupling effect. In vivo evaluation in a rat bone defect model reveals that the coated implants achieve 79.46% new bone volume fraction at 8 weeks post-implantation, with accelerated osseointegration, mature bone formation, and enhanced peri-implant innervation. By integrating corrosion regulation, bioactive ion delivery, and electroactive neuro-osteogenic modulation, this multifunctional coating provides a promising strategy for next-generation biodegradable orthopedic implants.

title: Delphinidin induces the upregulation of miR-23a-3p expression in skeletal muscle and miR-23a-3p release from intestinal cells.
abstract: Delphinidin, one of the major anthocyanidins, inhibits disuse muscle atrophy by increasing the expression of miR-23a-3p in mouse skeletal muscle. However, delphinidin is less stable and poorly absorbed in vivo, so its mechanism of function remains unclear. In this study, we aimed to elucidate the mechanism by which delphinidin increases miR-23a-3p expression in skeletal muscle. miRNAs can be packaged into extracellular vesicles (EVs) and secreted from cells. We investigated whether delphinidin induces the release of miR-23a-3p encapsulated in EVs from intestinal cells and whether these EVs increase miR-23a-3p expression in skeletal muscle cells. A single dose of delphinidin increased the expression of miR-23a-3p in the small intestine of mice. To examine whether delphinidin affects the secretion of miR-23a-3p in intestinal cells, we used differentiated Caco-2 cells as an in vitro model. Results showed that delphinidin increases the expression of miR-23a-3p in EVs secreted from differentiated Caco-2 cells. In addition, EVs derived from delphinidin-treated Caco-2 cells were taken up by differentiated C2C12 myotubes, resulting in increased intracellular miR-23a-3p expression. Our in vitro results suggest that intestinal cell-derived EVs may contribute to the antimuscle atrophy activity of delphinidin through the delivery of miR-23a-3p to skeletal muscle cells.

title: Myogenic differentiation-derived small extracellular vesicles as a therapeutic strategy for miR-193b-3p-mediated muscle regeneration.
abstract: The regeneration of skeletal muscle involves precisely regulated intercellular communication, including extracellular vesicle (EV)-mediated processes. In this study, we show that during in vitro myogenic differentiation of human skeletal muscle progenitor cells (myoblasts), miR-193b-3p accumulates within small EVs (sEVs) in a temporally regulated manner. Both sEV-mediated and synthetic delivery of miR-193b-3p enhanced myogenic differentiation in vitro and promoted histological recovery in a murine volumetric muscle loss model. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that miR-193b-3p directly suppresses adapter-related protein complex 2 subunit mu 1 (AP2M1), a clathrin-associated adapter protein that has not been well characterized in muscle biology, and identify it as a negative regulator of myogenic progression. AP2M1 knockdown phenocopied the effects of miR-193b-3p, suggesting that this regulatory axis may contribute to muscle regeneration. In addition, transcriptomic analyses of aged rodent and sarcopenic human datasets revealed conserved upregulation of AP2M1 in degenerative muscle states, supporting its potential clinical relevance. Collectively, these findings reveal a myogenic differentiation-dependent, sEV-mediated miRNA regulatory mechanism that contributes to muscle regeneration. Based on these results, we propose the miR-193b-3p-AP2M1 axis as a potential therapeutic target for muscle-wasting disorders.

title: Chaenomeles speciosa-derived extracellular vesicles accelerate fracture healing via orchestrating immuno-angiogenic coupling.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Fracture nonunion remains a major orthopaedic challenge, and dysregulation of the bone immune microenvironment is increasingly recognized as a key pathological driver. Chaenomeles speciosa is a medicinal plant with documented anti-inflammatory properties, making it a promising candidate for immune-modulatory therapy. This study investigated whether extracellular vesicles derived from Chaenomeles speciosa could reshape the immune microenvironment to promote fracture healing.
METHODS: Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed on human nonunion tissues to characterize cellular heterogeneity. Network pharmacology and molecular docking analyses were used to identify potential therapeutic targets of Chaenomeles speciosa. Extracellular vesicles were isolated by ultracentrifugation and characterized by transmission electron microscopy. Macrophage polarization, angiogenesis, and inflammatory signaling were assessed in vitro using RAW 264.7 macrophages and human umbilical vein endothelial cells. Bone regeneration was evaluated in a rat femoral fracture model using micro-computed tomography and histology.
RESULTS: Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed M1 macrophage dominance and enhanced M1-mediated communication with osteoblasts and endothelial cells in nonunion tissues. The IL-17 signaling pathway and matrix metalloproteinase-3 were identified as key therapeutic targets. Isolated extracellular vesicles exhibited excellent biocompatibility, promoted M2 macrophage polarization, attenuated inflammation, and enhanced angiogenesis in vitro. In the rat fracture model, treatment with these extracellular vesicles significantly accelerated bone regeneration, as evidenced by increased bone bridging and callus formation.
CONCLUSION: These findings establish a macrophage-centric pathological network in nonunion and demonstrate that Chaenomeles speciosa-derived extracellular vesicles promote bone repair through immuno-angiogenic coupling, supporting their potential as a multi-targeted therapeutic strategy for fracture healing.
